lectures.title: Introduction: hormones, feedback, hypothalamus & puberty
key: Hormone classes: peptides/proteins (membrane receptors, 2nd messengers), steroids & thyroid hormones (intracellular/nuclear receptors), amines
Negative feedback = the rule: the end hormone inhibits its pituitary and hypothalamic stimulators (long loop); short and ultrashort loops exist
Positive feedback: mid-cycle oestradiol → LH surge; oxytocin in labour
Level of the disease: PRIMARY (gland: end hormone and trophic hormone move in OPPOSITE directions), SECONDARY (pituitary), TERTIARY (hypothalamus) – both move in the SAME direction
Hypothalamus → portal system → anterior pituitary (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine); magnocellular neurons → posterior pituitary (ADH, oxytocin)
Anterior pituitary: GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH; PRL is the only one under tonic INHIBITION (dopamine)
Dynamic tests: suspect deficiency → STIMULATE; suspect excess → SUPPRESS
Puberty: girls 8–13 y (thelarche first), boys 9–14 y (testicular volume ≥ 4 mL first); precocious < 8 (girls) / < 9 (boys): central (GnRH-dependent) vs peripheral
Delayed puberty: constitutional delay (most common, bone age delayed), hypogonadotropic or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
traps: Primary disease: trophic hormone ↑ (opposite direction); secondary: both ↓
Precocious puberty → tall child but SHORT adult
ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, only stored in the posterior pituitary
gloss: pituitary hormone stimulating a peripheral gland

lectures.title: Pituitary: tumours, acromegaly, prolactinoma, hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus
key: Pituitary tumoral syndrome: headache, visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia), cranial nerve palsies (cavernous sinus), hypopituitarism, stalk effect (PRL ↑); MRI with gadolinium

Prolactinoma = most frequent adenoma: women – galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, infertility; men – decreased libido, impotence, macroadenoma; PRL > 200 ng/mL; DOPAMINE AGONISTS (cabergoline) first line even for macroadenomas

Acromegaly: GH adenoma; acral/facial enlargement, prognathism, diastema, sweating, arthropathy, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea, HT, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, colon polyps; diagnosis IGF-1 ↑ + GH not suppressed < 1 ng/mL on OGTT; treatment transsphenoidal surgery → somatostatin analogues → pegvisomant/cabergoline → radiotherapy

Hypopituitarism: tumours, surgery, radiotherapy, Sheehan (postpartum necrosis → agalactia), apoplexy, infiltrations, trauma; loss GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH; ACTH deficit = "white Addison" (pallor, no hyperkalaemia)
Replacement: hydrocortisone FIRST, then levothyroxine (follow FT4), sex steroids, GH, desmopressin

Diabetes insipidus: polyuria > 3 L, dilute urine; central (ADH ↓: surgery, trauma, tumours, idiopathic) vs nephrogenic (lithium, Ca ↑, K ↓); water deprivation + desmopressin test; treatment desmopressin (central), thiazides (nephrogenic)
GH deficiency in children: short proportional stature, delayed bone age, low IGF-1, low peak on 2 stimulation tests → recombinant GH
traps: Prolactinoma: medical treatment (cabergoline) BEFORE surgery, even with chiasm compression
OGTT SUPPRESSES GH normally (acromegaly: no suppression); hypoglycaemia (ITT) STIMULATES GH
Sheehan: low PRL (agalactia)
Water deprivation concentrates urine only in primary polydipsia
Diplopia = cavernous sinus invasion; field defect = chiasm

lectures.title: Thyroid: tests, goitre & nodules, cancer, thyroiditis, hypothyroidism
key: Tests: TSH first (best screening), FT4 (FT3); anti-TPO/anti-Tg (Hashimoto), TRAb (Graves); ultrasound; scintigraphy/uptake (only if TSH low); FNA (Bethesda)
Goitre: diffuse or nodular enlargement; iodine deficiency, Hashimoto, Graves; WHO grade 0–2; surgery for compression, retrosternal, suspicion of cancer
Nodule: TSH → if low, scintigraphy (hot = benign, autonomous); ultrasound risk (hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide) → FNA

Cancers: papillary (80 %, lymph nodes, best prognosis), follicular (blood → bone, lung), medullary (C cells, calcitonin, MEN2/RET), anaplastic (elderly, fatal); treatment thyroidectomy ± radioiodine, TSH suppression, Tg follow-up
Hashimoto: commonest cause of hypothyroidism, anti-TPO, firm goitre or atrophy, association with other autoimmune disease; lymphoma risk
Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: post-viral, painful thyroid, fever, ESR ↑, thyrotoxic phase with LOW uptake → NSAID/prednisone + β-blocker; then transient hypothyroidism
Painless/postpartum thyroiditis (TPO+), drug-induced (amiodarone, lithium, IFN, checkpoint inhibitors), Riedel (IgG4 fibrosis, stony goitre), acute suppurative (bacterial)

Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, myxoedema, Hertoghe sign, hyponatraemia, hypercholesterolaemia, CK ↑; levothyroxine (start low in elderly/coronary), target TSH (primary) or FT4 (central)
Myxoedema coma: hypothermia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, coma → IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone + ICU
traps: Never scintigraphy first in a nodule with normal TSH – it is ultrasound + FNA
Subacute thyroiditis: NO antithyroid drugs
Central hypothyroidism: monitor FT4, not TSH
Low-T3 with normal TSH = sick euthyroid
gloss: loss of the outer third of the eyebrows
parts: Lecture 3b – Goitre, nodules, thyroid cancer, thyroiditis

lectures.title: Thyrotoxicosis: Graves disease, toxic nodules, orbitopathy, thyroid storm
key: Thyrotoxicosis = excess circulating thyroid hormone; hyperthyroidism = overproduction (high uptake) – vs destructive thyroiditis/exogenous (low uptake)
Clinical: weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, tachycardia/AF, anxiety, insomnia, diarrhoea, proximal myopathy, osteoporosis, lid retraction
Graves: TRAb stimulate the TSH receptor; diffuse vascular goitre (bruit), orbitopathy, pretibial myxoedema, acropachy
Toxic adenoma / toxic multinodular goitre: hot nodules on scintigraphy with suppressed surrounding tissue; antibodies negative
Treatment: β-blockers + thionamides (methimazole/Thyrozol; PTU in 1st trimester and thyroid storm) 12–18 months; definitive: radioiodine (avoid with active orbitopathy, pregnancy) or thyroidectomy
Thionamide side effects: rash, arthralgia, hepatotoxicity (PTU), AGRANULOCYTOSIS (sore throat + fever → stop, CBC), hypothyroidism (dose), goitre
Graves orbitopathy (Werner NO SPECS, CAS activity): stop smoking, selenium (mild), IV methylprednisolone (active moderate–severe), radiotherapy, teprotumumab, decompression (optic neuropathy)
Thyroid storm: fever, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, agitation, vomiting → PTU, then iodine (1 h later), propranolol, hydrocortisone, cooling, ICU
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis: type 1 (iodine load on abnormal gland, high vascularity → thionamides ± perchlorate) vs type 2 (destructive → prednisone)
traps: Radioiodine in active orbitopathy only with steroid cover
Iodine in thyroid storm only AFTER thionamides
Secondary hyperthyroidism (TSHoma): TSH NOT suppressed
Diplopia = Werner class 4
gloss: clinical activity score of orbitopathy (≥ 3/7 active)
parts: Lab – Clinical activity score & Werner classification

lectures.title: Calcium & bone: hyper/hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D, osteoporosis
key: PTH: ↑ bone resorption, ↑ distal renal Ca reabsorption, ↓ phosphate reabsorption, ↑ 1α-hydroxylase (calcitriol) → ↑ gut absorption; calcitriol and Ca inhibit PTH

Primary hyperparathyroidism: women > 50, adenoma 85 %, hyperplasia (MEN1/2A); hypercalcaemia + high/inappropriate PTH + LOW phosphate; stones, bones (osteoporosis, osteitis fibrosa), abdominal groans (ulcer, pancreatitis, constipation), psychic moans
Surgery indications: symptomatic, Ca > 1 mg/dL above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones/nephrocalcinosis, eGFR < 60, hypercalciuria, age < 50; localisation by ultrasound + sestamibi
Hypercalcaemia PTH-independent: malignancy (PTHrP, metastases, myeloma), vitamin D intoxication, granulomas, thiazides, immobilisation; acute treatment IV saline + bisphosphonate
Secondary HPT: vitamin D deficiency, CKD (phosphate ↑, calcitriol ↓) → tertiary (autonomous)
Hypoparathyroidism: post-thyroidectomy (commonest), autoimmune (APS1), Mg deficiency; tetany, Chvostek, Trousseau, paresthesias, laryngospasm, seizures, cataract, basal ganglia calcification, long QT
Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH resistance (GNAS) – hypocalcaemia with HIGH PTH; type 1a with Albright osteodystrophy (short 4th metacarpal, round face, ossifications)
Acute hypocalcaemia: slow IV calcium gluconate 10 %; chronic: oral calcium + calcitriol/alfacalcidol

Osteoporosis: T-score ≤ −2.5 (DXA) or fragility fracture; risk factors (age, menopause, steroids, low BMI, smoking, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing); FRAX; calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonates/denosumab, teriparatide
traps: PHPT: phosphate is LOW
Pseudohypoparathyroidism: PTH HIGH
Tetany treatment is IV calcium gluconate (rebreathing only for hyperventilation)
Osteopenia is −1 to −2.5, osteoporosis ≤ −2.5
gloss: facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve
carpal spasm with BP cuff inflated

lectures.title: Adrenal: Addison, crisis, CAH, Cushing, hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma
key: Cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone – renin/K), fasciculata (cortisol – ACTH), reticularis (androgens); medulla (catecholamines)

Addison (primary): autoimmune 80 % (21-OH antibodies, APS2), TB, haemorrhage, metastases; fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, HYPERpigmentation, salt craving, Na ↓ K ↑, hypoglycaemia; cortisol ↓ ACTH ↑, Synacthen peak < 18 µg/dL
Treatment: hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses + fludrocortisone; sick-day rules (double/triple), emergency card, injectable kit; normal salt
Adrenal crisis: shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, Na ↓ K ↑ glucose ↓ → hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 200 mg/24 h + saline/glucose

CAH 21-hydroxylase deficiency: 17-OH-progesterone ↑, cortisol ↓, ACTH ↑, androgen ↑ → virilised 46,XX newborn, salt wasting crisis (day 7–14); non-classic: hirsutism; treatment glucocorticoid + fludrocortisone

Cushing syndrome: exogenous (most frequent) or endogenous: Cushing DISEASE (70 %), ectopic ACTH (SCLC, carcinoid), adrenal adenoma/carcinoma; central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, bruising, proximal myopathy, HT, diabetes, osteoporosis, depression

Cushing work-up: screening (1-mg DST, UFC, midnight salivary cortisol) → ACTH (dependent/independent) → high-dose DST + pituitary MRI / IPSS / CT; treatment surgery (transsphenoidal / adrenalectomy) or medical (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, pasireotide, mifepristone)
Primary aldosteronism: HT + hypokalaemia (only 30 %), metabolic alkalosis, renin suppressed, ARR ↑; adenoma (Conn) → adrenalectomy, bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone

Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache + sweating + palpitations + HT; metanephrines; α-blocker before β-blocker; 10 % rule outdated (≈ 40 % hereditary); incidentaloma work-up: cortisol (1-mg DST), metanephrines, ARR if HT
traps: Hyperpigmentation only in PRIMARY insufficiency
Replace cortisol before thyroxine
Never β-blocker before α-blocker in pheochromocytoma
Cushing disease suppresses on HIGH-dose dexamethasone; ectopic does not
Conn: renin LOW; secondary hyperaldosteronism: renin HIGH
gloss: corticotroph tumour growth after bilateral adrenalectomy
parts: Actions of glucocorticoids in endocrine disorders

lectures.title: Reproductive endocrinology: hypogonadism, Turner, Klinefelter, PCOS, amenorrhoea
key: Female axis: pulsatile GnRH → FSH (follicle growth, aromatase) and LH (theca androgens, ovulation, corpus luteum); oestradiol negative feedback except mid-cycle positive feedback
Male axis: LH → Leydig → testosterone; FSH + testosterone → Sertoli → spermatogenesis, inhibin B
Sex differentiation: SRY → testis → AMH (Müllerian regression) + testosterone (Wolffian → epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles) + DHT (external genitalia, prostate)

Hypogonadism: primary/hypergonadotropic (LH/FSH ↑: Klinefelter, Turner, POI, orchitis, chemotherapy) vs secondary/hypogonadotropic (LH/FSH ↓/N: Kallmann, prolactinoma, tumours, anorexia, stress, obesity)

Prepubertal onset: sexual infantilism, primary amenorrhoea, eunuchoid proportions; postpubertal: secondary amenorrhoea/hot flushes, loss of libido, regression of secondary sexual characters, osteoporosis
Turner 45,X: short stature, webbed neck, cubitus valgus, streak gonads, primary amenorrhoea, coarctation/bicuspid aorta, horseshoe kidney; GH + oestrogen–progestin
Klinefelter 47,XXY: tall, eunuchoid, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, azoospermia, high FSH/LH; testosterone replacement, TESE-ICSI

PCOS (Rotterdam 2/3): oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries; insulin resistance, obesity; LH/FSH ↑, SHBG ↓; lifestyle, combined pill, metformin, letrozole/clomiphene for fertility
Secondary amenorrhoea: pregnancy test → PRL, TSH → FSH/LH/E2 → progesterone challenge
traps: Kallmann = HYPOgonadotropic + anosmia
Turner: uterus PRESENT, short stature not due to GH deficiency
Klinefelter infertility cannot be treated with gonadotropins
First test in any secondary amenorrhoea: pregnancy test
gloss: arm span > height, lower segment > upper

lectures.title: Labs, dynamic tests, clinical cases & summaries
key: Stimulation tests (suspected deficiency): insulin tolerance test (GH + ACTH reserve), Synacthen (adrenal), glucagon/arginine/GHRH (GH), TRH, GnRH
Suppression tests (suspected excess): OGTT for GH (acromegaly), dexamethasone 1 mg overnight / 2 mg × 2 d / 8 mg (Cushing), saline infusion (aldosteronism), clonidine (pheochromocytoma)
Water deprivation + desmopressin: primary polydipsia vs central vs nephrogenic DI
Clinical case logic: symptoms → which axis → measure end hormone AND trophic hormone together → dynamic test → imaging LAST (incidentalomas are frequent)
traps: Imaging is never the first test in endocrinology
Interpret a hormone only with its regulator (TSH with FT4, PTH with Ca, ACTH with cortisol, renin with aldosterone)
parts: Student summary of the whole course

sx: Early breast/testicular development, pubic hair, growth spurt
ex: Tanner staging, growth velocity, testicular volume (> 4 mL = central in boys)
lab: LH/FSH (GnRH stimulation: LH peak > 5 = central), sex steroids, 17-OHP, hCG, TSH
img: Bone age (advanced), pelvic ultrasound, brain MRI if central (esp. boys)
tx: Central: GnRH agonist depot
Peripheral: treat cause (tumour, CAH)
oth: Central (GnRH-dependent): idiopathic (girls), CNS lesions (hamartoma); peripheral: McCune-Albright, CAH, tumours, testotoxicosis
paths.def: Signs of puberty before 8 years (girls) or 9 years (boys).

sx: Short stature, no pubertal signs
ex: Growth chart, anosmia (Kallmann), dysmorphism (Turner)
lab: LH/FSH (high = primary), sex steroids, PRL, TSH, IGF-1, karyotype
img: Bone age (delayed in constitutional delay), MRI if hypogonadotropic
tx: Constitutional: reassure ± short low-dose sex steroids
Hypogonadism: sex steroid induction
cx: DDx constitutional delay vs hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (difficult)
oth: Constitutional delay = most common, family history
paths.def: No breast development by 13 y (girls) or testicular enlargement by 14 y (boys).

sx: Headache, visual loss, diplopia
ex: Bitemporal hemianopia (confrontation), III/IV/VI palsies, optic atrophy
lab: Full pituitary hormone panel (PRL, IGF-1, cortisol, FT4, LH/FSH, sex steroids), Na/osmolality
img: Pituitary MRI with gadolinium; visual field (perimetry)
tx: Depends on type: cabergoline (prolactinoma), transsphenoidal surgery, radiotherapy
oth: DDx: craniopharyngioma (calcifications, children), meningioma, Rathke cyst, hypophysitis, metastases
paths.def: Local effects of a sellar mass, mostly macroadenomas (> 10 mm).

sx: Women: galactorrhoea, oligo/amenorrhoea, infertility
Men: low libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia, mass effects
ex: Galactorrhoea, visual fields if macro
lab: PRL (> 200 ng/mL suggests macroprolactinoma), exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, drugs, macroprolactin
tx: Cabergoline 0.25–0.5 mg twice weekly (first line), bromocriptine in pregnancy wish
Surgery if resistant/intolerant
cx: Hypogonadism → osteoporosis; tumour growth in pregnancy
oth: "Hook effect" in giant adenomas; stalk effect PRL < 100
paths.def: PRL-secreting adenoma, most frequent pituitary tumour.

sx: Headache, sweating, enlarged hands/feet (ring/shoe size), arthralgia, snoring, paraesthesia
ex: Coarse features, prognathism, diastema, macroglossia, thick oily skin, HT, goitre
lab: IGF-1 ↑, OGTT: GH not suppressed < 1 ng/mL; glucose, PRL, other axes
img: Pituitary MRI; echocardiography, colonoscopy, sleep study, thyroid US
tx: Transsphenoidal surgery
Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide), pegvisomant, cabergoline, radiotherapy
cx: Cardiomyopathy, HT, diabetes, sleep apnoea, colon cancer, arthropathy, carpal tunnel
oth: Mortality ×2 untreated; X-LAG / AIP in young gigantism
paths.def: GH excess after (acromegaly) or before (gigantism) epiphyseal closure, from a GH adenoma.

sx: Fatigue, pallor ("white Addison"), cold intolerance, amenorrhoea, loss of libido, agalactia (Sheehan)
ex: Pale, fine wrinkled skin, loss of body hair, hypotension
lab: Morning cortisol/ACTH, FT4 (TSH low/normal), LH/FSH with sex steroids, IGF-1, PRL, Na
tx: Hydrocortisone first → levothyroxine → sex steroids → GH; desmopressin if DI
oth: Causes: tumour, surgery, radiotherapy, Sheehan, apoplexy, hypophysitis, infiltrative, trauma
paths.def: Deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.

sx: Polyuria > 3 L, nocturia, intense thirst (preference for cold water)
ex: Dehydration if no access to water, hypernatraemia
lab: Urine osmolality < 300, plasma Na/osmolality high-normal; copeptin
img: Water deprivation + desmopressin test; MRI (absent posterior bright spot)
tx: Central: desmopressin
Nephrogenic: thiazide, low-salt diet, NSAIDs, stop lithium
oth: DDx primary polydipsia, osmotic diuresis (glucose), hypercalcaemia
paths.def: Polyuria of dilute urine from ADH deficiency (central) or renal resistance (nephrogenic).

sx: Short stature, low growth velocity, doll-like face, hypoglycaemia in infants
ex: Proportional short stature, truncal adiposity, micropenis (if gonadotropin deficit)
lab: Low IGF-1/IGFBP-3, 2 stimulation tests with peak < 7–10 ng/mL
tx: Recombinant GH daily until epiphyseal closure
cx: DDx: Turner, constitutional delay, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, skeletal dysplasia
oth: Normal intelligence
paths.def: Insufficient GH secretion in childhood (isolated or multiple).

sx: Often none; compression: dysphagia, dyspnoea, dysphonia
ex: Size (WHO grade), consistency, mobility, lymph nodes, Pemberton sign
lab: TSH (± FT4), anti-TPO, calcitonin (selected)
img: Ultrasound (TI-RADS), scintigraphy if TSH low, FNA (Bethesda)
tx: Benign: follow-up; compressive/large: surgery; toxic: radioiodine/surgery; malignant: thyroidectomy
oth: Risk: radiation, family history, male, extremes of age, hard fixed nodule, hoarseness
paths.def: Enlargement of the thyroid, diffuse or nodular; nodules are very common (US 50 % of elderly).

sx: Painless nodule, cervical nodes, hoarseness (late)
ex: Hard, fixed nodule, lymphadenopathy
lab: TSH, calcitonin + CEA (medullary), thyroglobulin after surgery
tx: Total thyroidectomy/lobectomy ± neck dissection; radioiodine ablation; TSH suppression
Medullary: surgery, RET testing
oth: Papillary best prognosis; anaplastic fatal
paths.def: Malignant tumours of follicular (papillary, follicular, anaplastic) or C cells (medullary).

sx: Hypothyroid symptoms or none
ex: Diffuse, firm, rubbery painless goitre or atrophy
lab: Anti-TPO (> 90 %), anti-Tg, TSH ↑ ± FT4 ↓
tx: Levothyroxine if hypothyroid (or subclinical with TSH > 10, pregnancy)
oth: Women 10:1; transient hashitoxicosis possible
paths.def: Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis.

sx: Neck pain radiating to the jaw/ear, fever, malaise, palpitations
ex: Exquisitely tender, firm thyroid
lab: ESR/CRP ↑↑, FT4 ↑ TSH ↓, antibodies negative
img: Very LOW radioiodine uptake ("white"), hypoechoic areas on US
tx: NSAIDs; prednisone 20–40 mg tapering if severe; β-blockers
oth: Triphasic: thyrotoxic → hypothyroid → euthyroid
paths.def: Post-viral granulomatous inflammation causing destructive thyrotoxicosis.

sx: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, menorrhagia, depression, slowness
ex: Dry cold skin, myxoedema, Hertoghe sign, bradycardia, slow-relaxing reflexes, hoarse voice
lab: TSH ↑ FT4 ↓ (primary); anti-TPO; Na ↓, cholesterol ↑, CK ↑, anaemia
tx: Levothyroxine 1.6 µg/kg/day (start 25 µg in elderly/coronary), check TSH after 6 weeks
Coma: IV T4 + hydrocortisone, warming, ventilation
cx: Myxoedema coma, coronary decompensation at treatment start
oth: Causes: Hashimoto, post-radioiodine/surgery, iodine deficiency, drugs (amiodarone, lithium)
paths.def: Thyroid hormone deficiency – primary (95 %) or central.

sx: Thyrotoxic symptoms, eye discomfort, diplopia
ex: Diffuse goitre with bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxoedema, acropachy, tremor, tachycardia
lab: TSH ↓, FT4/FT3 ↑, TRAb +
tx: β-blocker + thiamazole 12–18 months
Relapse: radioiodine (steroid cover if orbitopathy) or thyroidectomy
cx: AF, heart failure, osteoporosis, thyroid storm, orbitopathy
oth: Smoking worsens orbitopathy
paths.def: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism from stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies.

sx: Thyrotoxicosis (often milder, T3-predominant), elderly with AF
ex: Palpable nodule(s), no orbitopathy
lab: TSH ↓, FT4/FT3 ↑, antibodies negative
tx: Radioiodine or lobectomy/thyroidectomy after euthyroidism with thionamides
oth: Hot nodules are almost never malignant
paths.def: Autonomous hyperfunctioning nodule(s) (TSH-receptor activating mutations).

sx: Gritty eyes, tearing, photophobia, diplopia, decreased vision
ex: Lid retraction, lid lag, proptosis, chemosis, restriction (IR, MR), exposure keratitis
lab: TRAb (correlate with activity)
img: Hertel exophthalmometry, orbital CT/MRI (muscle bellies), CAS
tx: Stop smoking, euthyroidism, lubricants, selenium
Active moderate–severe: IV methylprednisolone, mycophenolate, teprotumumab, radiotherapy
Optic neuropathy: IV steroids ± decompression
oth: Werner NO SPECS classes 0–6; CAS ≥ 3/7 = active
paths.def: Autoimmune inflammation of orbital fat and extraocular muscles.

sx: Fever, agitation/delirium, vomiting, diarrhoea
ex: Tachycardia/AF, heart failure, jaundice
lab: FT4/FT3 ↑ (no threshold), Burch-Wartofsky score
tx: PTU (or methimazole), then iodine ≥ 1 h later, propranolol, hydrocortisone, cooling, supportive ICU
oth: Triggers: surgery, infection, radioiodine, iodine contrast, stopping drugs
paths.def: Life-threatening decompensated thyrotoxicosis.

sx: Often asymptomatic; fatigue, polyuria, constipation, depression, bone pain
ex: Kidney stones, fractures, HT
lab: Ca ↑, PTH ↑/inappropriately normal, phosphate ↓, urinary Ca ↑, 25-OH-D, creatinine, ALP
img: Neck US + 99mTc-sestamibi SPECT/CT (localisation), DXA (forearm), renal US
tx: Parathyroidectomy (indications)
Cinacalcet, bisphosphonates if not operable
cx: Osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, hypercalcaemic crisis; postoperative hungry bone
oth: DDx FHH (low urinary Ca), lithium, thiazides
paths.def: Autonomous PTH secretion (adenoma 85 %, hyperplasia, carcinoma).

sx: Polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, constipation, confusion, weakness
ex: Dehydration, short QT
lab: PTH, PTHrP, 25- and 1,25-vitamin D, SPEP, phosphate
tx: Hydration with saline, IV zoledronate, calcitonin, steroids (vitamin D, granulomas), denosumab, dialysis
oth: Malignancy = most common in hospital; PHPT in outpatients
paths.def: Corrected Ca > 10.5 mg/dL; PTH-dependent vs PTH-independent.

sx: Paraesthesias (perioral, fingers), cramps, tetany, seizures, laryngospasm
ex: Chvostek, Trousseau, cataract, dry skin, basal ganglia calcification
lab: Ca ↓, phosphate ↑, PTH low/inappropriately normal, Mg
tx: Acute: IV calcium gluconate 10 % slowly
Chronic: oral calcium + calcitriol (target low-normal Ca), rhPTH
oth: Causes: thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune (APS1), DiGeorge, hypomagnesaemia
paths.def: Insufficient PTH → hypocalcaemia with high phosphate.

sx: PHP: tetany; vit D: bone pain, proximal weakness
ex: Albright osteodystrophy (short 4th/5th metacarpals, round face, obesity, ossifications)
lab: PHP: Ca ↓ P ↑ PTH ↑↑; vit D deficiency: 25-OH-D < 20 ng/mL, Ca ↓/N, P ↓, PTH ↑, ALP ↑
tx: PHP: calcium + calcitriol
Vit D: cholecalciferol loading + maintenance
oth: Pseudo-PHP = AHO phenotype with normal calcium
paths.def: PTH resistance (GNAS) / insufficient vitamin D (osteomalacia, rickets).

sx: Silent until fracture: vertebral (height loss, kyphosis), hip, wrist
ex: Height loss, kyphosis
lab: Ca, P, 25-OH-D, PTH, TSH, creatinine, SPEP, testosterone (men) – secondary causes
tx: Calcium + vitamin D, exercise, fall prevention, stop smoking
Bisphosphonates (alendronate, zoledronate), denosumab, teriparatide/romosozumab (severe)
oth: Secondary: steroids, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing, PHPT, myeloma, malabsorption
paths.def: Low bone mass + microarchitectural deterioration → fragility fractures.

sx: Fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, salt craving, dizziness
ex: Hyperpigmentation (creases, scars, gums), orthostatic hypotension, vitiligo
lab: Na ↓ K ↑, glucose ↓, eosinophilia; morning cortisol ↓, ACTH ↑, renin ↑, aldosterone ↓; 21-OH antibodies
img: Synacthen test; adrenal CT (TB calcifications, haemorrhage, metastases)
tx: Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone; stress dosing; emergency card
oth: Autoimmune (APS2 with thyroid, T1DM), TB, HIV, haemorrhage (anticoagulants, meningococcus), adrenoleukodystrophy
paths.def: Destruction of both adrenal cortices (> 90 %).

sx: Vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, fever
ex: Hypotension/shock resistant to fluids
lab: Na ↓ K ↑ glucose ↓ (draw cortisol/ACTH but do not wait)
tx: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 50 mg/6 h, 0.9 % saline + glucose, treat cause
oth: Triggers: infection, surgery, stopping steroids, bilateral haemorrhage
paths.def: Acute life-threatening cortisol (± aldosterone) deficiency.

sx: Newborn: ambiguous genitalia (girls), salt-wasting crisis at 1–3 weeks
Later: precocious pseudopuberty, hirsutism, infertility
ex: Virilisation, accelerated growth
lab: 17-OH-progesterone ↑↑ (newborn screening), ACTH ↑, renin ↑, Na ↓ K ↑
tx: Hydrocortisone (children) / prednisone, dexamethasone; fludrocortisone + salt; genital surgery
cx: Short adult height, adrenal crisis, testicular adrenal rest tumours
oth: Forms: salt-wasting, simple virilising, non-classic
paths.def: Autosomal recessive defect of cortisol (± aldosterone) synthesis with androgen excess.

sx: Weight gain, weakness, easy bruising, depression, oligomenorrhoea, decreased libido
ex: Moon face, plethora, buffalo hump, central obesity, purple striae > 1 cm, proximal myopathy, HT, hirsutism, acne
lab: 1-mg DST > 1.8 µg/dL, UFC ↑, late-night salivary cortisol ↑; ACTH; high-dose DST; K ↓ in ectopic
img: Pituitary MRI, IPSS, adrenal CT, thoraco-abdominal CT/DOTATATE PET
tx: Transsphenoidal surgery (disease), adrenalectomy (adrenal), resect ectopic source
Ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, pasireotide, mifepristone; bilateral adrenalectomy
cx: Diabetes, HT, osteoporosis, infections, thrombosis, psychosis
oth: Pseudo-Cushing: alcohol, depression, obesity
paths.def: Chronic glucocorticoid excess.

ex: HT, no oedema
lab: K ↓ (30–50 %), metabolic alkalosis, ARR ↑ with suppressed renin; confirm (saline infusion)
tx: Unilateral: laparoscopic adrenalectomy
Bilateral: spironolactone/eplerenone
cx: Cardiovascular and renal damage beyond BP
oth: Most common cause of secondary hypertension
paths.def: Autonomous aldosterone secretion: adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia.

ex: Paroxysmal or sustained HT, orthostatic hypotension, weight loss
lab: Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines; genetic testing
tx: α-blocker (phenoxybenzamine, doxazosin) → β-blocker → volume → laparoscopic surgery

oth: Hereditary: MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx

lab: 1-mg DST (autonomous cortisol), metanephrines, ARR if HT/hypokalaemia

oth: Primary: Klinefelter, cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemo; secondary: Kallmann, prolactinoma, opioids, obesity

questions.q: Which of the following is/are not a hormone of the anterior pituitary gland:
questions.note: Vasopressin (ADH) and oxytocin are hypothalamic hormones STORED in and released from the POSTERIOR pituitary. Anterior: GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH.

questions.q: The following statements about precocious puberty are TRUE:

o.t: It is the appearance of sexual developments before the age of 9 years old in boys and 8 years old in girls
Complete precocious puberty can be idiopathic
It is characterized by tall final stature
Incomplete contrasexual precocious puberty in males is characterized by excess of androgens
Incomplete precocious puberty is characterized by HPT–HPF maturation

questions.note: Precocious puberty: < 8 y girls, < 9 y boys; central (GnRH-dependent, often idiopathic in girls) or peripheral; tall stature in childhood but SHORT final height (early epiphyseal closure); contrasexual in boys = feminisation; incomplete (peripheral) forms lack HPG maturation.

questions.q: Which of the following are anterior pituitary hormones?
questions.note: Anterior pituitary: GH, PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH. ADH = hypothalamus/posterior pituitary; cortisol = adrenal; LHRH (GnRH) = hypothalamus.

questions.q: The following are anterior pituitary hormones:
questions.note: Anterior pituitary: FSH, LH, prolactin, GH, TSH, ACTH. PTH = parathyroid; GHRH = hypothalamus; IGF-1 = liver.

questions.q: The hypothalamic-pituitary system consists of:
questions.note: Hypothalamus + pituitary stalk with the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system (to the anterior pituitary) + neurohypophysis (axonal tract to the posterior pituitary). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hormones secreted by the hypothalamus are:
questions.note: Hypothalamus: TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine (PIF), ADH and oxytocin. STH = GH from the anterior pituitary. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) are:
questions.note: Anterior pituitary: GH (STH), PRL, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH. ADH – hypothalamus/posterior pituitary; somatostatin – hypothalamus; somatomedin (IGF-1) – liver. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which of the following are causes of PERIPHERAL precocious puberty?
questions.note: Peripheral (GnRH-independent) precocious puberty: gonadal tumours (Leydig/Sertoli, granulosa), testotoxicosis (activating LH-receptor mutation), McCune–Albright (GNAS), CAH, adrenal tumours, hCG-secreting tumours, severe primary hypothyroidism. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A patient is diagnosed with a pituitary macroadenoma following an MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region performed for persistent headache syndrome. The patient also reports diplopia. We can therefore affirm that:

o.t: The tumor compresses the optic chiasm
The tumor has invaded the cavernous sinus
The tumor compresses the internal carotid artery
The tumor has affected the oculomotor nerves
The diplopia is not related to the extension of the macroadenoma

questions.note: Diplopia means the macroadenoma has extended laterally into the cavernous sinus and compresses the oculomotor nerves (III, IV, VI). Chiasm compression gives visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia), not diplopia; the carotid is usually encased without symptoms.

questions.q: In a patient with pituitary dwarfism, the following clinical and hormonal findings are present:

o.t: An elevated IGF-1 value and a glucose stimulation test for GH shows the inability of GH to rise above 7 ng/mL

questions.note: GH deficiency (pituitary dwarfism): low IGF-1, harmonious (proportional) short stature, delayed bone age, normal intelligence; diagnosis by stimulation tests (insulin, arginine, glucagon) with GH peak < 7–10 ng/mL.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man is hospitalized for decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, headache, and diplopia. MRI shows a pituitary tumor measuring 26/24/14 mm (AP/LL/CC), with invasion of the cavernous and sphenoidal sinuses and distortion of the optic chiasm. Prolactin is 8024 µIU/mL (N: 98–456 µIU/mL). The first-line treatment is:
questions.note: Macroprolactinoma (PRL > 8000), even invasive with chiasm compression: dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are first line – rapid shrinkage and visual recovery. Surgery only for resistance/intolerance or apoplexy with persistent deficit.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy is diagnosed with panhypopituitarism. The most important pituitary deficiency that must be substituted first is:
questions.note: In hypopituitarism replace ACTH (cortisol) FIRST, then TSH: giving levothyroxine before hydrocortisone can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

questions.q: The most common type of pituitary adenoma is:
questions.note: Prolactinomas are the most frequent (≈ 40 %) pituitary adenomas, then non-functioning adenomas (≈ 30 %), GH, ACTH, TSH (rare).

questions.q: Which of the following is/are used in the paraclinical diagnosis of acromegaly?

o.t: Lateral plain film of the skull

questions.note: Acromegaly: diagnosis = IGF-1 + OGTT (GH not suppressed < 1 ng/mL); imaging of the sella (MRI; skull X-ray shows an enlarged sella); screening of comorbidities: colonoscopy (polyps, cancer), thyroid ultrasound (goitre/nodules), echocardiography, sleep study. (Colonoscopy is for complications, not diagnosis.)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions plays a role in the etiology of hyperprolactinemia besides a prolactinoma?
questions.note: Non-tumoural hyperprolactinaemia: pregnancy/lactation, drugs (dopamine antagonists: neuroleptics, metoclopramide, oestrogens), stalk compression, primary hypothyroidism (TRH), chronic renal failure, cirrhosis, PCOS, chest wall lesions. Sheehan's necrosis gives LOW prolactin (agalactia).

questions.q: The following are clinical features of acromegaly:

o.t: Enlargement of the nose, jaw malocclusion and widely spaced teeth

questions.note: Acromegaly: coarse features, enlarged nose/lips/tongue, prognathism with malocclusion and spaced teeth, frontal bossing, large hands/feet, oily skin, acne, skin tags, hyperhidrosis. No exophthalmos. (Hertoghe sign = lateral eyebrow loss in hypothyroidism.)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions are accompanied by hyperprolactinemia?

o.t: Postpartum ischemic necrosis of the pituitary

questions.note: Hyperprolactinaemia: stalk compression (disconnection), renal failure, PCOS, dopamine-antagonist drugs, hypothyroidism, pregnancy. Postpartum pituitary necrosis (Sheehan) → hypoprolactinaemia.

questions.q: Diabetes insipidus is characterized by:

o.t: Urine is more diluted than normal
There is an excess of vasopressin
Treatment of the nephrogenic form consists of hormonal substitution
Water deprivation test is used to differentiate between the central and the nephrogenic form

questions.note: Diabetes insipidus: polyuria of DILUTE urine (low osmolality), lack of ADH (central) or renal resistance (nephrogenic); water deprivation + desmopressin test distinguishes central (responds) from nephrogenic. Nephrogenic DI is treated with thiazides/NSAIDs, not ADH.

questions.q: Which of the following imagistic investigations are used for a patient with acromegaly?

o.t: Pituitary MRI is the procedure of choice
Lateral plain film of the skull (focused on the sella turcica)

questions.note: Imaging in acromegaly: pituitary MRI with gadolinium (method of choice); lateral skull X-ray may show an enlarged/double-floor sella. OGTT and hormone dosages are laboratory tests; colonoscopy is a complication screening.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the pituitary gland are TRUE?

o.t: The posterior pituitary produces ADH and oxytocin
Vasopressin secretion is stimulated by both smoking and alcohol
The most frequent pituitary tumors are prolactin-producing tumors
In pituitary adenomas, hormone production is always correlated with tumor dimension

questions.note: Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin; prolactinomas are the most frequent adenomas; primary hypothyroidism (high TRH) raises PRL. Alcohol INHIBITS ADH; hormone secretion is not proportional to tumour size.

questions.q: The substitution of which pituitary hormone deficits is for life?
questions.note: Lifelong replacement: ACTH (hydrocortisone), TSH (levothyroxine), gonadotropin deficiency (sex steroids, at least until the age of natural menopause/andropause). GH in adults is optional/individualised; PRL is not replaced.

questions.q: The following are neurological signs of pituitary adenomas:
questions.note: Pituitary mass effects: headache, chiasm compression (bitemporal hemianopia), raised ICP/hydrocephalus (vomiting), temporal lobe invasion (seizures), cavernous sinus invasion/thrombosis (diplopia). Impotence is endocrine (hypogonadism/hyperprolactinaemia).

questions.q: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is caused by:
questions.note: Nephrogenic DI: hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia, lithium, chronic kidney disease, congenital V2/aquaporin-2 defects. Pituitary surgery, sarcoidosis, head trauma and craniopharyngioma cause CENTRAL DI.

questions.q: The following statements about pituitary insufficiency are TRUE:

o.t: It can develop after pituitary surgery or radiotherapy
The initial clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome is agalactia
Sheehan syndrome is caused by ischemic pituitary necrosis
ACTH insufficiency is characterized by hyperpigmentation

questions.note: Hypopituitarism: GH and gonadotropins fail first (TSH and ACTH last); after surgery/radiotherapy; Sheehan = postpartum ischaemic necrosis presenting with agalactia and failure to resume menses. ACTH deficiency gives PALLOR ("white Addison").

questions.q: What are the clinical features of pituitary microadenoma?

o.t: Seldom, signs of pituitary insufficiency possibl

questions.note: MICROadenomas (< 10 mm) give hormonal syndromes but no mass effect: no chiasm or oculomotor compression, rarely headache or pituitary insufficiency. DI is rare in adenomas.

questions.q: Choose the right answers about acromegaly:

o.t: The main cause of acromegaly is pituitary adenoma secreting somatoliberin
The PRL dosage is not useful
In the hyperglycemia test (OGTT), in patients with acromegaly, GH is decreased below 1 ng/ml
In the medical treatment of acromegaly dopamine agonists could be used

questions.note: Acromegaly: GH-secreting adenoma (not somatoliberin); gigantism only before epiphyseal closure; PRL is co-secreted in 30 % (useful); GH is NOT suppressed < 1 ng/mL on OGTT; dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are an option for mild disease.

questions.q: A patient with pituitary dwarfism has the following clinical and hormonal characteristics:

o.t: Low IGF-1 and an insufficient GH response (GH < 10 ng/ml) within the OGTT

questions.note: GH deficiency: low IGF-1, insufficient GH peak on stimulation (< 7–10 ng/mL), delayed bone age, PROPORTIONAL segments (ratio ≈ 1), normal intelligence.

questions.q: Pasireotide:

o.t: Is a first generation somatostatin receptor ligand
Is a second generation somatostatin receptor ligand
It can be used in the treatment of acromegaly
It can be used in the treatment of Cushing's disease
It can cause disturbances of the glucose metabolism

questions.note: Pasireotide = second-generation (multireceptor, SSTR5) somatostatin analogue, used in acromegaly and Cushing's disease; causes hyperglycaemia.

questions.q: Treatment of pituitary insufficiency in adults consists of:
questions.note: Adult hypopituitarism: hydrocortisone (ACTH), levothyroxine (TSH), sex steroids, ± GH, desmopressin for DI. TSH and prolactin are not administered; cabergoline treats prolactinomas.

questions.q: The treatment of choice for a patient with a microprolactinoma is:
questions.note: Microprolactinoma: dopamine agonist (cabergoline first, bromocriptine in pregnancy wish).

questions.q: The following represent possible causes of hyperprolactinemia:
questions.note: Hyperprolactinaemia: pregnancy, oestrogens/oral contraceptives, dopamine antagonists, hypothyroidism, CKD. Bromocriptine LOWERS prolactin; Sheehan gives low PRL; hyperthyroidism does not raise PRL.

questions.q: The first two pituitary deficiencies that need to be substituted in a patient with panhypopituitarism:
questions.note: The two vital deficiencies to replace first are ACTH (hydrocortisone first) and TSH (levothyroxine after cortisol).

questions.q: Methods of treatment for acromegaly include the following:
questions.note: Acromegaly: transsphenoidal surgery (first line), somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide), pegvisomant, cabergoline, radiotherapy.

questions.q: Acromegaly is manifested by:

o.t: Downward and forward growth of the mandible

questions.note: Acromegaly: prognathism (mandible grows down and forward), large hands and feet, carpal tunnel acroparaesthesias, large ears/nose/lips; weight GAIN of soft tissues rather than loss.

questions.q: Pituitary dwarfism has the following clinical and hormonal features:

o.t: Stimulation testing shows that GH cannot rise above 10 ng/mL

questions.note: GH deficiency: GH peak < 7–10 ng/mL on stimulation tests (insulin, arginine, glucagon – the oral glucose test SUPPRESSES GH and is used for acromegaly), low IGF-1, proportional short stature, delayed bone age, normal intelligence. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the correct answers about acromegaly:

o.t: The main cause of acromegaly is a pituitary adenoma secreting somatostatin
Increased PRL indicates compression of the optic chiasm
In acromegaly, during the glucose tolerance test, GH stays above 1 ng/mL
In the medical treatment of acromegaly, dopamine agonists can be used

questions.note: Acromegaly = GH-secreting adenoma; diagnosis: high IGF-1 + GH not suppressed below 1 ng/mL (0.4 with sensitive assays) on OGTT. PRL may be co-secreted or raised by stalk compression (not chiasm compression). Treatment: surgery, somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant, cabergoline. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 57-year-old man with heart failure and severe sleep apnoea is referred for sweating, fatigue, constipation and hyperprolactinaemia. Exam: prognathism, thick hands, coarse facial features, thick skin. Initial tests: anaemia, low TSH and low FT4.

o.t: The best test for the definitive diagnosis is the glucose suppression test with GH measurement
The best test for the definitive diagnosis is pituitary MRI
Somatostatin analogues are the most appropriate treatment in this case
The most appropriate treatment in this case is trans-sphenoidal surgery
Cabergoline is the most appropriate treatment in this case

questions.note: Acromegaly (with central hypothyroidism = macroadenoma causing hypopituitarism): diagnosis = IGF-1 + OGTT (GH not suppressed). With severe heart failure and sleep apnoea the anaesthetic risk is high → medical treatment with somatostatin analogues first (they also improve cardiomyopathy/apnoea); surgery later if feasible. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Visual involvement in the pituitary tumour syndrome:

o.t: Is most often due to compression of the optic chiasm
Fundus examination always shows papilloedema from intracranial hypertension
Ocular motility can be affected when a tumour compresses the oculomotor nerves
The visual field defect is most often a bitemporal hemianopia
Visual involvement is more frequent with microadenomas

questions.note: Macroadenomas with suprasellar extension compress the chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia (superior quadrants first); lateral (cavernous) extension → III, IV, VI palsies; papilloedema is exceptional; late optic atrophy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In a pituitary tumour, frontal and lateral X-rays of the sella turcica show:

o.t: Demineralisation of its walls, sometimes erosions
Deformation of its contours, sometimes their disappearance
Intra- or suprasellar calcifications suggesting craniopharyngioma

questions.note: Plain skull X-ray (historical): ballooned/enlarged sella, thinned eroded walls and clinoids, double floor (asymmetric growth), calcifications typical of craniopharyngioma. MRI is now the method of choice. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Microadenomas:

o.t: Have by definition a diameter below 10 mm
Can deviate the pituitary stalk laterally

questions.note: Microadenoma < 10 mm, seen on MRI from 2–4 mm as a hypo-intense lesion with delayed enhancement, may deviate the stalk or bulge the diaphragm; usually functioning (prolactinoma, ACTH). Calcifications suggest craniopharyngioma. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Causes of functional (non-tumoural) hyperprolactinaemia include:
questions.note: Physiological (stress, pregnancy, breastfeeding, sleep), drugs (neuroleptics, metoclopramide, domperidone, antidepressants, opiates, oestrogens, verapamil), hypothyroidism (high TRH), renal failure. Thyroid hormone does not raise PRL (it corrects hypothyroid hyperprolactinaemia). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Medical treatment of prolactinoma:

o.t: Bromocriptine is given in large "loading" doses
The efficacy of bromocriptine on prolactin is very low
Bromocriptine can reduce the size of adenomas

questions.note: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline first choice, bromocriptine) normalise PRL in most patients and shrink the tumour; started at LOW doses, increased progressively (nausea, orthostatic hypotension). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical signs of acromegaly include:

o.t: Dysmorphic syndrome predominating at the extremities
Thickening of the skin and subcutaneous tissue

questions.note: Acromegaly: acral and facial dysmorphia, prognathism with diastema, thick oily skin, hyperhidrosis, macroglossia, deep voice, sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel, arthropathy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Complications of acromegaly are:
questions.note: Acromegaly: hypertension, cardiomyopathy/heart failure, diabetes, sleep apnoea, colon polyps/cancer, goitre, arthropathy, HYPERCALCIURIA → kidney stones. (Gallstones are a side effect of somatostatin analogue THERAPY, not of the disease.) (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: True statements:

o.t: Gonadotroph adenomas are often invasive macroadenomas
Gonadotroph adenomas are usually discovered by galactorrhoea
Thyrotroph adenomas present with hypothyroidism and goitre
Non-secreting adenomas can destroy the neighbouring normal pituitary, causing pituitary insufficiency

questions.note: Gonadotroph adenomas are clinically non-functioning macroadenomas discovered by mass effect; corticotroph → Cushing's disease; thyrotroph (TSHoma) → HYPERthyroidism with goitre; non-functioning macroadenomas compress the normal gland → hypopituitarism. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In the long term, a patient with pituitary insufficiency is threatened by:
questions.note: Untreated hypopituitarism: hypoglycaemia (GH + cortisol deficit), bradycardia/arrhythmias (hypothyroidism), hypotension, HYPOthermia, hypopituitary coma (cortisol + thyroid deficit) triggered by stress. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Causes of pituitary insufficiency include:

o.t: Congenital malformations (midline syndromes) causing severe childhood hypopituitarism

questions.note: Hypopituitarism: tumours (adenomas, craniopharyngioma), surgery/radiotherapy, Sheehan, apoplexy, infiltrations (haemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, histiocytosis), hypophysitis, trauma, congenital (PROP1, septo-optic dysplasia). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Polyuria–polydipsia syndromes:

o.t: Polyuria is defined as a urine output above 2.5–3 L/24 h
Polyuria is defined as more than 10 voids/day
Primary polydipsia can occur in psychiatric states
Nephrogenic polyuria can occur in lithium intoxication
In hypothalamic (central) diabetes insipidus there is an ADH deficiency

questions.note: Polyuria = > 3 L/24 h (> 40–50 mL/kg) – frequency is pollakiuria; causes: central DI (ADH deficit), nephrogenic DI (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia), primary (psychogenic) polydipsia, osmotic diuresis (diabetes). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The water deprivation test (positive if urine volume falls and osmolality rises):

o.t: Is positive in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Is positive in hypothalamic diabetes insipidus
Is negative in hypothalamic diabetes insipidus

questions.note: Water deprivation: primary polydipsia concentrates urine (positive); in central and nephrogenic DI the urine stays dilute (negative); desmopressin then concentrates urine only in CENTRAL DI. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In the treatment of hypothalamic (central) diabetes insipidus we use:
questions.note: Central DI: desmopressin (DDAVP, intranasal/oral/sublingual); in partial forms drugs that enhance ADH release/action (carbamazepine, chlorpropamide, thiazides historically). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Ophthalmological signs of the pituitary tumour syndrome are:

o.t: Chiasmal compression by an infrasellar lesion

questions.note: Pituitary tumours compress the chiasm from BELOW by SUPRAsellar extension (bitemporal hemianopia) and the oculomotor nerves by lateral (cavernous) extension. Aphasia is not an ocular sign. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Causes of the pituitary tumour syndrome:
questions.note: Sellar masses: adenomas (most), craniopharyngioma, meningioma, glioma, Rathke cleft cyst, metastases, hypophysitis, granulomas (sarcoid, TB), abscess, aneurysm. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Imaging of the pituitary tumour syndrome:

o.t: Decreased size of the sella turcica

questions.note: Gadolinium-enhanced pituitary MRI is the method of choice; CT shows bone erosion and calcifications (craniopharyngioma); the sella is ENLARGED; microadenomas are frequent. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Acral dysmorphism, prognathism, frontal bossing, wide nose and organomegaly indicate which diagnosis?
questions.note: Classic acromegalic dysmorphism (GH/IGF-1 excess) with visceromegaly. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of hormonal deficiencies (hypopituitarism):

o.t: Therapy does not require specific replacement
The order has no real importance
The first to be treated is the corticotroph deficiency
In children, GH deficiency should be treated before the gonadal deficiency
In children, thyroid deficiency should be replaced after GH

questions.note: Replace cortisol first, then thyroxine, then GH (children) and sex steroids (induce puberty at the appropriate age, after GH has optimised growth). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In hypothalamic-pituitary (central) diabetes insipidus we find all the following EXCEPT one:
questions.note: Central DI: ADH (copeptin) is LOW; dilute urine, high-normal plasma osmolality and sodium, polyuria, thirst. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Water restriction is effective only in:
questions.note: Only primary (psychogenic/dipsogenic) polydipsia concentrates the urine and resolves with water restriction. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman is hospitalized for palpitations, hypersudation, fever, tremors, and pain on palpation of the anterior neck. Lab results show TSH < 0.005 µIU/mL, FT4 = 26 pmol/L (N: 12–22 pmol/L), elevated ESR. Thyroid ultrasound shows diffuse changes in the right lobe. Treatment will include:
questions.note: Painful neck + fever + high ESR + transient thyrotoxicosis = subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: NSAIDs or prednisone in decreasing doses + β-blockers. No antithyroid drugs (destructive, not hyperfunction), no radioiodine (uptake is low).

questions.q: The initial treatment of subacute thyroiditis with transient hyperthyroidism includes:

o.t: Corticosteroids in forms with significant inflammatory syndrome and hyperalgesic forms

questions.note: Subacute thyroiditis: β-blockers for thyrotoxic symptoms + anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs; corticosteroids if severe pain/inflammation). Antithyroid drugs and surgery are useless; levothyroxine only in the later hypothyroid phase.

questions.q: Hashimoto's thyroiditis:

o.t: Is a frequent cause of central hypothyroidism

questions.note: Hashimoto thyroiditis: most frequent cause of PRIMARY hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas, mainly women; anti-TPO/anti-Tg antibodies, firm diffuse goitre or atrophy.

questions.q: Mark the correct statements for treatment of hypothyroidism:

o.t: In the elderly and in patients with underlying coronary artery disease, we begin the treatment with full dose requirement
The goal is to return TSH concentrations to normal in primary hypothyroidism
In central hypothyroidism, TSH is the index for adequate replacement
Calcium channel blockers may be associated with hormone replacement treatment to protect for tachycardia

questions.note: Hypothyroidism: lifelong levothyroxine; start LOW (12.5–25 µg) and go slow in the elderly/coronary patients; target = normal TSH in primary hypothyroidism; in central hypothyroidism follow FT4 (TSH is useless).

questions.q: Choose the correct statement:

o.t: In acute thyroiditis etiology can be both bacterial and viral
In subacute thyroiditis the patient can present symptoms of hypothyroidism at onset
Hashimoto's thyroiditis may progress to hypothyroidism
Hashimoto's thyroiditis may associate other autoimmune diseases such as pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes mellitus
In acute thyroiditis, prednisone is the first- choice treatment

questions.note: Hashimoto progresses to hypothyroidism and associates other autoimmune diseases (APS2: Addison, T1DM, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo). Acute (suppurative) thyroiditis is bacterial → antibiotics/drainage; subacute thyroiditis starts with a THYROTOXIC phase.

questions.q: Regarding Hashimoto thyroiditis the next statements are TRUE:

o.t: It is always characterized by hypothyroidism
Corticotherapy is the treatment of choice, given the fact that it is an autoimmune disorder
In evolution, the patients can develop hyperthyroidism
High anti-TPO and antithyroglobulin antibodies are suggestive for the diagnosis
It is associated with other autoimmune diseases

questions.note: Hashimoto: high anti-TPO/anti-Tg, may show a transient thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis), associated autoimmune diseases; not always hypothyroid (euthyroid goitre possible); treatment = levothyroxine if hypothyroid, NOT corticosteroids.

questions.q: Thyroiditis can be induced by the following drugs:
questions.note: Drug-induced thyroiditis: amiodarone (type 2 AIT), lithium (painless thyroiditis), interferon-α, immune checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

questions.q: Myxedema coma is characterized by:
questions.note: Myxoedema coma: HYPOthermia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoventilation with CO2 retention, bradycardia, stupor/coma – high mortality → IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone.

questions.q: In lymphocytic thyroiditis or Hashimoto are true the following:

o.t: The presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies is possible
The presence of anti-receptor antibodies for TSH is pathognomonic

questions.note: Hashimoto: anti-TPO (> 90 %) and anti-Tg antibodies, diffuse firm painless goitre, evolution to hypothyroidism and atrophic forms. TRAb are characteristic of Graves.

questions.q: Antibodies anti-TPO are elevated even if TSH is normal.

o.t: There is associated auto-immune Addison disease in MEN type II
Must be followed by regular TSH measures

questions.note: Positive anti-TPO with normal TSH = euthyroid autoimmune thyroiditis: risk of progression to hypothyroidism (~4 %/year) → periodic TSH. Addison belongs to APS type 2, not MEN.

questions.q: Subacute thyroiditis is manifested by:

o.t: High titers of antibodies against TSH-receptor
Thyroid ultrasonography – hypoechoic aspect corresponding to the affected area
High titers of antibodies against TPO

questions.note: Subacute thyroiditis: painful tender (often asymmetrical) enlarged thyroid, fever, high ESR, ill-defined hypoechoic areas, LOW uptake; antibodies are absent or low.

questions.q: Central hypothyroidism is characterized by:
questions.note: Central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism: low FT4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH.

questions.q: Myxedema coma is characterized by:
questions.note: Myxoedema coma: hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypercapnia, stupor/coma.

questions.q: The following statements about Hashimoto's thyroiditis are TRUE:

o.t: It is more often found in men
Patients need to be monitored for other endocrine/nonendocrine autoimmune conditions
In evolution, patients can occasionally present with thyrotoxicosis
High titers of anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies are most striking laboratory findings
It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism

questions.note: Hashimoto: mostly women, most common cause of hypothyroidism, high anti-TPO/anti-Tg, possible transient hashitoxicosis, association with other autoimmune diseases (monitoring).

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient has a high FT4 and a low TSH. Anti-Tg and anti-TPO antibodies are positive and TRAb are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Thyrotoxicosis (high FT4, low TSH) with anti-TPO/anti-Tg but NO TRAb = the transient thyrotoxic phase of Hashimoto thyroiditis (hashitoxicosis). TSHoma would have inappropriately normal/high TSH. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Ultrasound features of BENIGN thyroid nodules are:

o.t: A thin, regular hypoechoic peripheral halo

questions.note: Low-risk (benign) features: iso/hyperechoic, spongiform or purely cystic, well-defined smooth margins, thin regular halo. Suspicious: marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide, irregular/infiltrative margins, thick or absent halo, central vascularity (TI-RADS/EU-TIRADS). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis the following are true:

o.t: Positive anti-TPO antibodies and progression to hypothyroidism
The presence of TSH-receptor antibodies is mandatory
The goitre is diffuse, firm and painless
It may evolve to atrophic forms

questions.note: Hashimoto: autoimmune, anti-TPO (± anti-Tg), diffuse firm painless (rubbery) goitre or atrophic form, slow evolution to HYPOthyroidism. TRAb are typical of Graves. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: About goitre:

o.t: Any diffuse or localised enlargement of the thyroid is a goitre
Goitres are very frequent, especially in men
After thyroidectomy the patient is treated with iodine for life
Goitres are more frequent in iodine-overloaded regions

questions.note: Goitre = enlarged thyroid (diffuse or nodular), much more frequent in WOMEN, endemic in iodine-DEFICIENT areas. Compressive goitres → surgery; after total thyroidectomy → levothyroxine (not iodine). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The diagnostic orientation depends on the clinical characteristics of the goitre:
questions.note: Examine volume (WHO grade), consistency (soft, firm, hard/stony), nodules, pain (subacute thyroiditis), mobility on swallowing (fixed = invasive cancer, Riedel), lymph nodes, compressive signs. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Biological tests needed for the diagnosis of a nodular goitre are:
questions.note: Nodular goitre: TSH first (low → scintigraphy for hot nodule), anti-TPO/anti-Tg (Hashimoto), calcitonin (medullary carcinoma screening, debated), ultrasound and FNA of suspicious nodules. Iodine levels and ESR are not routine. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The thyroid secretes:
questions.note: Follicular cells → T4 (and some T3); parafollicular C cells → calcitonin. TSH = pituitary; PTH = parathyroids. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Signs suggestive of hypothyroidism are:
questions.note: Hypothyroidism: fatigue, somnolence, COLD intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, dry cold pale (yellowish) skin, myxoedema, hoarse voice, slow reflexes. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Coronary insufficiency in hypothyroidism:

o.t: Its tolerance is decreased by the frequent anaemia
Is often paucisymptomatic while the patient is hypothyroid
Risks decompensating when treatment is started

questions.note: Hypothyroidism favours atherosclerosis (HYPERcholesterolaemia, diastolic HT); angina is often silent (low O2 demand) and may worsen when levothyroxine is started → start low (12.5–25 µg) and go slow. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of hypothyroidism:

o.t: Doses must be increased progressively every month
The dose is divided into three daily intakes
The right dose is the one that normalises TSH

questions.note: Levothyroxine once daily on an empty stomach (long half-life), started low and increased every 4–6 weeks according to TSH (young healthy patients can start at full dose ~1.6 µg/kg). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In subacute thyroiditis:

o.t: The aetiology is bacterial or fungal
The thyroid is enlarged, firm and very painful on palpation
ESR is high (50–100 mm or more)
Half of cases show signs of hypothyroidism

questions.note: De Quervain subacute thyroiditis: post-VIRAL, painful tender goitre, fever, very high ESR/CRP, initial thyrotoxic phase, blank scintigraphy (very low uptake), later transient hypothyroidism. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of subacute thyroiditis uses:

o.t: Corticosteroids in hyperalgesic forms with marked inflammation

questions.note: NSAIDs/aspirin, β-blockers for thyrotoxic symptoms, prednisone for severe forms; no thionamides; levothyroxine only for a symptomatic hypothyroid phase. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis:

o.t: The evolution is chronic and may lead to hypothyroidism
The goitre is diffuse, firm, rubbery, painless
The presence of anti-peroxidase antibodies is pathognomonic
Other endocrine deficits may be associated (adrenal, ovarian insufficiency)

questions.note: Hashimoto: autoimmune, chronic, firm rubbery goitre, hypothyroidism, associated APS2 diseases. Anti-TPO are very sensitive but NOT pathognomonic (also in Graves and healthy people). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical manifestations of hypothyroidism:

o.t: Hertoghe sign (loss of the outer third of the eyebrows)

questions.note: Hypothyroidism: slowness, apathy, cold dry skin, myxoedema (non-pitting oedema), Hertoghe sign, hoarse voice, macroglossia, bradycardia. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Management of thyroid enlargement (goitre):

o.t: If of medium size – ultrasound only
If of medium size – abstention with clinical monitoring

questions.note: Small euthyroid goitre: surveillance; medium: surveillance (± levothyroxine/iodine in deficiency) with TSH, ultrasound, FNA of suspicious nodules; plunging/compressive goitre: thyroidectomy + replacement. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Signs of Riedel thyroiditis:
questions.note: Riedel (IgG4-related) thyroiditis: rare, invasive fibrosis, woody/stony fixed goitre with compression, usually euthyroid (may become hypothyroid); mimics anaplastic carcinoma but is not linked to it. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Low T3, normal T4 and normal TSH – what is your diagnosis?
questions.note: Low T3 with normal TSH/T4 = non-thyroidal illness ("sick euthyroid", low-T3 syndrome) from reduced deiodinase activity; amiodarone and steroids/propranolol also inhibit T4→T3 conversion. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Myxoedema coma:
questions.note: Myxoedema coma: rare, extreme decompensated hypothyroidism (elderly, cold, infection, sedatives) with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia – mortality up to 30–40 %. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: De Quervain thyroiditis:

o.t: Is characterised by preceding general (flu-like) signs

questions.note: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis: post-viral, prodromal flu-like illness, painful goitre, high ESR, blank scintigraphy (no uptake). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In hypothyroidism, hormone tests show:

o.t: Normal or low TSH (in secondary forms)

questions.note: Hypothyroidism: low FT4; primary → high TSH; central → low/inappropriately normal TSH; high TRH in primary hypothyroidism may raise prolactin. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The following statements about thyroid ophthalmopathy are true:

o.t: Diplopia and ophthalmoplegia can be part of the clinical presentation
Its severity is correlated with anti-TPO antibody levels
It is characterized by exophthalmos and ptosis
It can cause vision loss due to alteration of the optic chiasm

questions.note: Graves orbitopathy: proptosis, lid retraction, restrictive myopathy (diplopia, ophthalmoplegia), compressive optic NEUROPATHY at the orbital apex; treated with IV glucocorticoids. Severity correlates with TRAb (not anti-TPO); there is lid retraction, not ptosis.

questions.q: The potential side effects of treatment with synthetic antithyroid drugs are:
questions.note: Thionamides (thiamazole/Thyrozol, PTU): goitrogenic effect, hepatitis (PTU) / cholestasis (methimazole), iatrogenic hypothyroidism reversible on dose reduction, leukopenia → agranulocytosis, rash, arthralgia. Vocal cord palsy is a surgical complication.

questions.q: A hormonal profile consisting of elevated or normal TSH + elevated FT4 suggests:
questions.note: Inappropriately normal/high TSH with high FT4 = central hyperthyroidism (TSH-secreting adenoma) or thyroid hormone resistance (differentiated by TRH test, α-subunit, MRI, genetics).

questions.q: The following features are found in thyrotoxicosis:

o.t: Heat intolerance, loss of appetite, constipation

questions.note: Thyrotoxicosis: heat intolerance with INCREASED appetite, diarrhoea/frequent stools, tremor, hyperreflexia, tachycardia, irritability/insomnia, upper lid retraction, weight loss, hyperglycaemia tendency.

questions.q: According to Werner's classification, diplopia is a feature of Graves orbitopathy class:
questions.note: Werner (NO SPECS): 0 no signs, 1 only signs (lid retraction), 2 soft tissue, 3 proptosis, 4 EXTRAOCULAR MUSCLES (diplopia), 5 cornea, 6 sight loss.

questions.q: The following statements about laboratory findings in hyperthyroidism are false:

o.t: In secondary hyperthyroidism TSH is low and FT4 is elevated
In toxic adenoma, thyroid scintigraphy reveals a hot nodule with low or absent function of the contralateral lobe
TSH receptor antibodies are present in both Graves disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Bradycardia is a common finding on ECG

questions.note: FALSE: in SECONDARY hyperthyroidism TSH is high/normal (not low); TRAb are typical of Graves (rare blocking antibodies in some Hashimoto); TACHYcardia/AF, not bradycardia. Toxic adenoma = hot nodule with suppressed rest of the gland (true).

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient with Graves disease complaining of diplopia is classified as Werner class:
questions.note: Diplopia (extraocular muscle involvement) = Werner class 4 (classes are 0–6).

questions.q: Regarding the ophthalmopathy that occurs in Graves disease, the next statements are FALSE:

o.t: It is always bilateral and symmetrical
Proptosis > 22 mm is classified as class 3 Werner
Sight loss is mostly due to ischemia of the optic nerve

questions.note: FALSE: topical steroids are useless (IV methylprednisolone); orbitopathy is often asymmetric (unilateral in 10 %); proptosis classes are not defined at > 22 mm in Werner (class 3 = proptosis ≥ 3 mm above normal); sight loss is due to COMPRESSIVE optic neuropathy (apex crowding), or corneal ulcer. It is autoimmune inflammation (true).

questions.q: Clinical aspects that are specific for hyperthyroidism are:
questions.note: Hyperthyroidism: weight loss despite increased appetite, tachycardia/AF, irritability, anxiety, tremor, heat intolerance; wide pulse pressure with high SYSTOLIC (low diastolic) pressure. Non-pitting oedema (myxoedema) = hypothyroidism (pretibial in Graves).

questions.q: Potential side effects of treatment with synthetic antithyroid drugs are:

o.t: Hypothyroidism, reversible upon discontinuation of treatment

questions.note: Antithyroid drugs: goitrogenic, hepatitis, reversible hypothyroidism if over-dosed, leukopenia/agranulocytosis.

questions.q: A 39-year-old woman diagnosed with Graves disease 8 years ago, on medical treatment with Thyrozol 10 mg/day, is admitted for palpitations, sweating, tremor, palpebral edema, chemosis, double vision, excessive tearing. Her blood tests reveal: TSH < 0.005 microIU/ml, FT4 = 39 nmol/L (N: 12–22 nmol/L). The best treatment options are:

o.t: "Block and replace therapy": Thyrozol and L- Thyroxine

questions.note: Relapsing/persistent Graves after 8 years of thionamides = definitive treatment. With ACTIVE moderate-severe orbitopathy (chemosis, diplopia) radioiodine can worsen the eyes unless given with steroid cover – thyroidectomy (after euthyroidism) or radioiodine + prednisone are the options.

questions.q: An 81-year-old male patient with a long history of atrial fibrillation presents with palpitations, sweating, weight loss, restlessness. TSH is decreased (undetectable), FT4 = 37 pmol/L (N = 12–22 pmol/L), low radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU). The following disorders should be considered in this case:
questions.note: Elderly patient with AF (on amiodarone) + thyrotoxicosis with LOW uptake: amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (type 2 destructive) – or type 1 on pre-existing nodular/Graves disease (uptake may be low because of iodine load). Subacute thyroiditis would be painful.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man is presenting with palpebral edema, congestion of the conjunctiva, convergent strabismus, exophthalmos (proptosis: 20 mm). TSH receptor antibodies are detected in high titres while TSH is low. According to Werner's classification, he has thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy grade? The best treatment option is:
questions.note: Convergent strabismus/diplopia = extraocular muscle involvement → Werner class/grade IV; active moderate-severe orbitopathy → IV methylprednisolone (pulse therapy), with antithyroid drugs for the hyperthyroidism.

questions.q: Which of the following statements related to toxic thyroid adenoma are true?

o.t: Anti-thyroglobulin and anti-TPO antibodies are negative
Scintigraphy appears as a cold nodule
The option of choice is substitution with levothyroxine followed by surgery (total lobectomy)
Thyroid scintigraphy is useless for diagnosis

questions.note: Toxic adenoma (Plummer): antibody negative, HOT nodule with suppressed extranodular tissue on scintigraphy (essential for diagnosis); treatment = radioiodine or lobectomy after euthyroidism with antithyroid drugs (never levothyroxine).

questions.q: The followings represent therapeutic options for hyperthyroidism:
questions.note: Hyperthyroidism: thionamides (thiamazole/Thyrozol, propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine, thyroidectomy (+ β-blockers). Levothyroxine and external radiotherapy are not treatments.

questions.q: Radioactive iodine treatment:

o.t: Is not effective in Graves' disease
Can be effective in active oedematous Graves' disease (orbitopathy)
Is not a treatment of choice in toxic adenoma
Its effect is slow, over weeks/months
Is indicated in subacute thyroiditis with hyperthyroidism

questions.note: Radioiodine is effective in Graves (relapse, after antithyroid drugs) and is a treatment of choice for toxic adenoma/toxic multinodular goitre; its effect takes 6–12 weeks (months). It is avoided (or covered by steroids) in active orbitopathy and useless in subacute/destructive thyroiditis (low uptake). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which statements about toxic thyroid adenoma are true?

o.t: Anti-thyroglobulin and anti-TPO antibodies are negative
The treatment of choice is levothyroxine followed by surgery (total lobectomy)
Thyroid scintigraphy is useless for diagnosis

questions.note: Toxic adenoma (Plummer): autonomous HOT nodule with suppressed TSH and extinction of the rest of the gland, antibodies negative; treatment = radioiodine or lobectomy after making the patient euthyroid with antithyroid drugs. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hyperthyroidism:

o.t: Results from hypersecretion of thyroid hormones
Is caused by hypersecretion of TSH
Graves' disease is of autoimmune origin
Graves' disease is due to stimulating immunoglobulins bound to the TSH receptor
Toxic thyroid adenomas are extremely rare

questions.note: Hyperthyroidism = excess thyroid hormone production; Graves = autoimmune, stimulating TRAb on the TSH receptor (the original item says "thyroxine receptor" – it is the TSH receptor). TSH-secreting adenomas are rare; toxic adenomas are relatively common. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Signs suggestive of hyperthyroidism are:

o.t: Rapid weight loss with increased appetite

questions.note: Thyrotoxicosis: weight loss despite increased appetite, HEAT intolerance, sweating, tachycardia/AF, fine tremor, nervousness, insomnia. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The evolutive risks of Graves' disease are:
questions.note: Graves complications: thyrotoxic heart disease (AF, heart failure – especially elderly), malignant (oedematous) orbitopathy, osteoporosis, thyroid storm, and late hypothyroidism (spontaneous or after treatment). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In the hyperthyroidism of Graves' disease, hormone tests show:
questions.note: Graves: high FT4/FT3 with suppressed TSH and positive TRAb. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In the treatment of hyperthyroidism we use:
questions.note: Thionamides, radioiodine, thyroidectomy, β-blockers (symptomatic, propranolol also lowers T4→T3 conversion). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Synthetic antithyroid drugs:

o.t: Act on all peroxidase-dependent steps of thyroid hormone synthesis
Treatment is started at low doses that are progressively increased
Agranulocytosis is a very rare but very serious side effect

questions.note: Thionamides block TPO-dependent iodide organification and coupling; started at HIGH (attack) doses then tapered (or block-and-replace); euthyroidism after 3–6 weeks; agranulocytosis (< 0.5 %) is rare but severe (stop if fever/sore throat); hypothyroidism is dose-dependent and reversible. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Radioactive iodine treatment:

o.t: Is indicated in Graves' disease relapsing after surgery
Should have limited indication in Graves' disease because it can worsen ophthalmopathy
Is a treatment of choice in toxic adenoma

questions.note: Radioiodine: relapse after drugs or surgery, toxic adenoma/multinodular goitre; works over 2–6 months; can worsen active orbitopathy (steroid cover); useless in iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (low uptake) and contraindicated in pregnancy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Subtotal (near-total) thyroidectomy can be used:

o.t: Mainly in Graves' disease relapsing after stopping antithyroid drugs
In exceptional cases of severe iodine-induced hyperthyroidism

questions.note: Thyroidectomy: relapsing Graves (especially large goitre, orbitopathy, pregnancy wish), toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma (lobectomy), severe amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis resistant to treatment. Not for small euthyroid goitres. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The risks of subtotal thyroidectomy are:

o.t: Relapse if the resection is too limited
Permanent hypothyroidism if the resection is too wide

questions.note: Thyroidectomy complications: hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcaemia), recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (dysphonia, bilateral → dyspnoea), haemorrhage/haematoma, recurrence (subtotal) or hypothyroidism. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of severe Graves' ophthalmopathy uses:

o.t: Partial tarsorrhaphy when lid closure is incomplete
Cyclosporine A, alone or with corticosteroids

questions.note: Severe/active TED: IV methylprednisolone pulses, cyclosporine/mycophenolate, teprotumumab, orbital radiotherapy; decompression surgery for optic neuropathy or after inactivation; tarsorrhaphy/lubricants for exposure. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Graves orbitopathy:

o.t: Involves the extra-ocular tissues of the orbital cone

questions.note: Thyroid eye disease: autoimmune inflammation of orbital fat and extraocular muscles (TSH-receptor/IGF-1R), mostly with Graves; can threaten vision (compressive optic neuropathy, corneal ulcer); exophthalmos > 18–20 mm on Hertel. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hyperthyroidism:

o.t: No need to measure T3, T4

questions.note: Primary hyperthyroidism: high FT4 ± FT3 with suppressed TSH. CPK is LOW in hyperthyroidism (high in hypothyroidism). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which diseases induce hyperthyroidism?
questions.note: Thyrotoxicosis: Graves, toxic adenoma/MNG, TSHoma, destructive thyroiditis (de Quervain, painless, postpartum), transient hashitoxicosis, iodine/amiodarone. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Thyroid storm (acute thyrotoxic crisis):

o.t: Is a benign, moderate state often occurring in thyroiditis

questions.note: Thyroid storm: life-threatening decompensated thyrotoxicosis (fever > 40 °C, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, agitation, GI symptoms) triggered by surgery, infection, radioiodine – mortality 10–20 % → PTU, iodine (after thionamide), β-blockers, steroids, ICU. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Management of iodine-induced hyperthyroidism:

o.t: Beta-blockers if the cardiac condition allows

questions.note: Iodine/amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis: stop iodine if possible; type 1 → thionamides (± perchlorate); type 2 (destructive) → prednisone 0.5–0.7 mg/kg; β-blockers if tolerated (heart); thyroidectomy for severe refractory forms. Radioiodine is useless (low uptake). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which condition must you suspect first in front of weight loss with preserved appetite?
questions.note: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite = hyperthyroidism (or uncontrolled diabetes). Adrenal insufficiency and malignancy cause anorexia. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 58-year-old female patient, a smoker, is referred due to a right femoral neck fracture following a fall from her own height.

o.t: Vitamin D treatment is not necessary if a bisphosphonate is indicated
Bone densitometry shows a density below -2 standard deviations if osteoporosis is present
Elevated PTH always indicates a concomitant risk of kidney stones
You advise the patient to stop smoking

questions.note: A low-energy (fragility) femoral neck fracture defines severe (established) osteoporosis, whatever the BMD; stopping smoking is part of treatment. Vitamin D (+ calcium) is always given with bisphosphonates. Densitometric osteoporosis is a T-score ≤ −2.5 SD (not −2). Raised PTH is not "always" a lithiasis risk (secondary HPT).

questions.q: The clinical manifestations of hypoparathyroidism include:
questions.note: Hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcaemia: tetany, paraesthesias, cramps, Chvostek/Trousseau, basal ganglia calcification, CATARACT (chronic). Kidney stones and gastritis/ulcer belong to HYPERparathyroidism.
