questions.q: A 17-year-old adolescent presents with short stature, obesity, round face, intellectual delay, brachydactyly, short metacarpals, subcutaneous ossifications, muscle cramps. Calcium is decreased. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.note: Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, round face, obesity, short 4th–5th metacarpals, subcutaneous ossifications, mental delay) + hypocalcaemia with HIGH PTH = pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a (PTH resistance, GNAS).

questions.q: A 31-year-old woman with a history of recurrent acute pancreatitis and constipation is referred to endocrinology due to repeatedly elevated calcium values found on routine tests.

o.t: The most useful test is 25(OH)VitD dosage
The most useful test is PTH dosage
Parathyroid scintigraphy is the mandatory confirmatory test
Surgery is the conservative treatment of choice in this case
The patient can be managed conservatively (medically)

questions.note: Hypercalcaemia: the key next test is PTH (high/inappropriately normal = primary hyperparathyroidism). Scintigraphy (sestamibi) only LOCALISES before surgery; symptomatic PHPT (pancreatitis) → parathyroidectomy.

questions.q: Which of the following is/are element(s) of hypoparathyroidism?
questions.note: Hypoparathyroidism: tetany, paraesthesias, cramps, (posterior sub)capsular cataract, basal ganglia calcifications, prolonged QT. Stones and peptic ulcer = hyperparathyroidism.

questions.q: Which are the biological effects of PTH?

o.t: Increases Ca reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubules

questions.note: PTH: ↑ distal tubular Ca reabsorption, ↓ phosphate reabsorption, ↑ bone resorption, ↑ renal 1α-hydroxylase → 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D (which ↑ intestinal absorption). 25-hydroxylation is hepatic and not PTH-regulated.

questions.q: Which of the following are elements of the clinical picture of primary hyperparathyroidism?
questions.note: Primary hyperparathyroidism: "stones, bones, groans, moans" – nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis/osteitis fibrosa, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, constipation, neuropsychiatric signs, hypertension. Tetany and cataract = hypoparathyroidism.

questions.q: Which disorders are elements of the MEN 1 syndrome?
questions.note: MEN 1 (menin): Parathyroid hyperplasia, Pituitary adenoma, Pancreatic/duodenal NETs (3 P). MEN 2: medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma (+ HPT in 2A).

questions.q: Which of the following are sites of the effects of PTH?
questions.note: PTH acts directly on bone and kidney; the intestinal effect is indirect, via calcitriol.

questions.q: A 34-year-old patient with a history of kidney stones, pancreatitis, and hypertension is referred to your clinic for further investigations. What is the most probable diagnosis and what tests would you recommend?
questions.note: Kidney stones + pancreatitis + hypertension = primary hyperparathyroidism → serum (ionised) calcium and PTH.

questions.q: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by:

o.t: Low calcium and low PTH levels
It can be caused by a vitamin D deficiency
It can progress into tertiary hyperparathyroidism

questions.note: Secondary hyperparathyroidism: physiological PTH rise in response to low/normal calcium – vitamin D deficiency, CKD (high phosphate), malabsorption; may become autonomous (tertiary). Treatment: vitamin D/calcitriol, phosphate BINDERS (not phosphate), cinacalcet. Osteomalacia occurs with vitamin D deficiency, not in all.

questions.q: Amongst the causes of secondary endocrine osteoporosis are:
questions.note: Secondary osteoporosis: endocrine (Cushing/glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, diabetes), myeloma, malabsorption, drugs. Postmenopausal osteoporosis is primary; osteogenesis imperfecta is genetic.

questions.q: Treatment of tetany crisis consists of:
questions.note: Hypocalcaemic tetany: slow IV calcium gluconate 10 % (10–20 mL over 10 min, then infusion), correct magnesium; then oral calcium + active vitamin D. Rebreathing is for hyperventilation (normocalcaemic) tetany.

questions.q: A 17-year-old female adolescent presents with short stature, obesity, round face, mental retardation, brachydactyly, shortened metacarpals, subcutaneous ossifications, muscle cramps. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.note: Albright osteodystrophy + hypocalcaemia = pseudohypoparathyroidism.

questions.q: Clinical manifestations of hypoparathyroidism are:
questions.note: Hypoparathyroidism: tetany, cramps, paraesthesia, cataract (chronic).

questions.q: Possible causes of hypocalcemia are:
questions.note: Hypocalcaemia: post-thyroidectomy/neck surgery hypoparathyroidism, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, CKD. Hypothyroidism is not a cause.

questions.q: The following statements about acute hypocalcemia are TRUE:

o.t: It is manifested by carpopedal spasm
Should be treated with calcium supplements orally
Should be treated by calcium gluconate 10% by slow IV infusion
It is manifested by systemic metastatic calcification
It is caused by acute kidney injury

questions.note: Acute hypocalcaemia: carpopedal spasm, tetany, laryngospasm, seizures → slow IV calcium gluconate 10 %. Metastatic calcification = hyperphosphataemia/hypercalcaemia; AKI is not a typical cause.

questions.q: Useful investigations for primary hyperparathyroidism are:
questions.note: Primary hyperparathyroidism: total/ionised calcium + intact PTH (diagnosis), 25-OH vitamin D, renal function and urinary calcium (complications); localisation by neck ultrasound and 99mTc-sestamibi SPECT/CT before surgery.

questions.q: A 42-year-old patient with recurrent kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, hypertension and constipation is referred to your clinic. Considering the most probable diagnosis, which laboratory findings are expected?
questions.note: Primary hyperparathyroidism: high total/ionised calcium, high intact PTH, hypercalciuria, low phosphate.

questions.q: Imaging and laboratory tests useful in evaluating primary hyperparathyroidism:

o.t: Hypercalcaemia and HYPERphosphataemia with raised PTH

questions.note: PHPT work-up: calcium + PTH (hypercalcaemia with HYPOphosphataemia), 24-h urinary calcium, 25-OH vitamin D, renal ultrasound (stones/nephrocalcinosis), DXA (forearm especially), localisation by ultrasound + sestamibi before surgery. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Primary hyperparathyroidism:

o.t: Is the most frequent cause of hypocalcaemia
Is more frequent after 50 and in women
Is due to inappropriate PTH production by an adenoma of the chief cells
Or to diffuse hyperplasia of the 4 glands or multiple adenomas in a multiple endocrine neoplasia

questions.note: PHPT: most frequent cause of HYPERcalcaemia in outpatients; women > 50 y; single adenoma (85 %), hyperplasia (MEN1/2A), carcinoma (< 1 %); treatment = parathyroidectomy (indications) or monitoring/cinacalcet. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Signs of hyperparathyroidism are:
questions.note: PHPT: nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis with fragility fractures, osteitis fibrosa cystica, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, CONSTIPATION, polyuria, neuropsychiatric symptoms. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Primary hyperparathyroidism:
questions.note: PHPT: mild hyperchloraemic acidosis (PTH reduces bicarbonate reabsorption), adenoma visible on neck ultrasound, high alkaline phosphatase (bone turnover); treatment is surgical when indicated. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hypocalcaemia:

o.t: Is most often of parathyroid origin
Chvostek and Trousseau signs are found

questions.note: Hypocalcaemia: hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical most often), vitamin D deficiency, CKD, hypomagnesaemia, pancreatitis; neuromuscular excitability – Chvostek, Trousseau ("main d'accoucheur"), carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, seizures. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Symptoms of the hypercalcaemic syndrome are:
questions.note: Hypercalcaemia: fatigue, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, constipation, polyuria-polydipsia (nephrogenic DI), confusion, headache, SHORT QT and arrhythmias, pruritus (calcium deposition). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Osteoporosis:

o.t: Is an increased skeletal fragility linked to decreased bone mineral content
Treatment relies on magnesium and sunlight

questions.note: Osteoporosis: low bone mass + microarchitecture deterioration → fragility fractures; T-score ≤ −2.5 (−1 to −2.5 = osteopenia); risk factors: age, female sex, low BMI, smoking, steroids, early menopause; treatment: calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonates/denosumab/teriparatide. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Inappropriately increased PTH secretion causes all the following EXCEPT one:
questions.note: PTH lowers renal phosphate reabsorption → HYPOphosphataemia; it raises calcium, urinary calcium and bone resorption. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Chronic hypercalcaemia may cause all the following EXCEPT one:
questions.note: Hypercalcaemia: constipation, polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic DI), weakness, confusion → coma; it does not cause diabetes MELLITUS. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Only one statement about the effects of PTH is correct:
questions.note: PTH ↑ distal calcium reabsorption, ↓ phosphate (and bicarbonate) reabsorption in the proximal tubule – hence a mild hyperchloraemic acidosis – and ↑ 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D. (Intermittent PTH/teriparatide is anabolic, but continuous PTH resorbs bone.) (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman presents with weight loss, decreased appetite, nausea, progressive cutaneous hyperpigmentation, arterial hypotension, and anemia. On admission, Na+ = 128 mmol/L (N: 136–145 mmol/L), basal cortisol = 5 µg/dL (N: 5–20 µg/dL). What findings do you expect on an extended workup?

o.t: Elevated TSH in the presence of type 1 autoimmune polyendocrinopathy
Decreased ACTH due to possible pituitary insufficiency

questions.note: Primary adrenal insufficiency: insufficient Synacthen peak (< 18 µg/dL), low DHEA-S, high renin (mineralocorticoid deficit), HIGH ACTH (hyperpigmentation). Autoimmune thyroid disease belongs to APS type 2 (Schmidt), not type 1 (candidiasis + hypoparathyroidism + Addison).

questions.q: In a patient with suspected Cushing's disease:

o.t: Aldosterone is elevated and renin is increased
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is necessary in all cases
If ACTH is normal, the diagnosis is ruled out
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test brings cortisol below normal
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test does not suppress cortisol

questions.note: In Cushing's DISEASE (pituitary ACTH adenoma) the high-dose dexamethasone test (Liddle 2×8) suppresses cortisol by > 50 %; ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours do not suppress. ACTH is normal or high; aldosterone/renin are not part of the work-up.

questions.q: Specify the diagnoses according to the following hormonal and biochemical profile: slightly elevated ACTH, normal serum cortisol at 8h, elevated serum cortisol at 24h, plasma cortisol after Liddle 2×8 test decreased by less than 50% of basal cortisol at 8 hours.
questions.note: ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism that does NOT suppress by > 50 % on high-dose dexamethasone = ectopic (paraneoplastic) ACTH secretion. Cushing's disease suppresses; adrenal causes have suppressed ACTH.

questions.q: Choose the correct answers regarding the treatment of Addison's disease:

o.t: Hydrocortisone must be continued for life
Hydrocortisone must be accompanied by a salt-free diet
Treatment monitoring is based on dietary regimen
Treatment monitoring is based on plasma cortisol
The dose must be increased in case of stress

questions.note: Addison treatment: lifelong hydrocortisone (15–25 mg/day) + fludrocortisone; double/triple the dose in stress (sick-day rules); NORMAL/liberal salt intake; monitoring is clinical (weight, BP, well-being), not by plasma cortisol.

questions.q: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, the early-onset form (in utero), is characterized by:

o.t: Decreased cortisol, elevated ACTH, decreased 17-OH progesterone
In girls: pseudo-hermaphroditism (virilized external genitalia with female internal organs)
No sodium loss in urine or dehydration

questions.note: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency: low cortisol, high ACTH and very high 17-OH-progesterone → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, virilised external genitalia in 46,XX girls with normal internal organs (female pseudohermaphroditism), salt wasting (dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia) in 75 %; glucocorticoid (dexamethasone/hydrocortisone) "freinage" corrects the androgen excess.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with weight loss, decreased appetite, progressive cutaneous hyperpigmentation, arterial hypotension, headache, hypoglycemia. On admission Na+ = 121 nmol/L (N: 136–145 mmol/L), basal cortisol = 3 µg/dL (VN: 7–22 µg/dL) and 60 min after Synacthen 250 micrograms IV = 7 µg/dL.

o.t: The most likely diagnosis is primary adrenocortical insufficiency
The most likely diagnosis is hypercortisolism
An additional useful investigation is ACTH dosage

questions.note: Hyperpigmentation + hypotension + hyponatraemia + hypoglycaemia + low cortisol with insufficient Synacthen response = primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison); ACTH (high) confirms the primary origin. Treatment: hydrocortisone, normal salt intake. Ketoconazole lowers cortisol.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about adrenocortical insufficiency are FALSE?

o.t: Hyperpigmentation is the classical finding in secondary adrenocortical insufficiency
Weakness, fatigue, postural hypotension are common
Acute adrenocortical insufficiency (adrenal crisis) is characterized by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, increased urea and creatinine levels
Acute adrenocortical insufficiency (adrenal crisis) is characterized by hypernatremia, hypokalemia, low urea and creatinine levels
Plasma ACTH is elevated in secondary adrenocortical insufficiency

questions.note: FALSE statements: hyperpigmentation belongs to PRIMARY insufficiency (high ACTH/POMC); adrenal crisis = HYPOnatraemia, HYPERkalaemia, raised urea/creatinine; ACTH is LOW in secondary insufficiency.

questions.q: Etiology of Addison's disease includes:
questions.note: Addison causes: autoimmune adrenalitis (≈ 80 %), tuberculosis, other infections (HIV, fungi), metastases, bilateral haemorrhage (anticoagulants, meningococcaemia), adrenoleukodystrophy, bilateral adrenalectomy. Fludrocortisone is a treatment.

questions.q: Cushing's disease defines:

o.t: A syndrome caused by therapy with large doses of prednisone

questions.note: Cushing's DISEASE = ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (≈ 70 % of endogenous Cushing's syndrome).

questions.q: Which of the following statements are correct? In central adrenocortical insufficiency:

o.t: Dexamethasone is the treatment of choice
Restriction of sodium is absolutely indicated
It's forbidden to interrupt the treatment no matter the cause
Imagistic assessment of the pituitary is recommended

questions.note: Secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency: hydrocortisone (not dexamethasone), no salt restriction, mineralocorticoids NOT needed (aldosterone is renin-dependent), lifelong treatment that must not be stopped, and pituitary MRI to find the cause.

questions.q: The clinical features characteristic for Cushing syndrome are:
questions.note: Cushing: CENTRAL (truncal) obesity with thin limbs, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, easy bruising, infections, HYPERtension, diabetes, osteoporosis, myopathy, depression/psychosis, hirsutism, acne, oligomenorrhoea.

questions.q: A 50-year-old patient, overweight, with high blood pressure, headaches, hyperpigmentation, abdominal red-purple striae. You suspect:
questions.note: Hypertension, overweight, purple abdominal striae = Cushing's syndrome; hyperpigmentation suggests an ACTH-dependent form (ectopic ACTH, Cushing's disease).

questions.q: Mark the FALSE statements:

o.t: Cushing disease is caused by adrenal adenoma secreting cortisol
Liddle test 2×2 distinguishes pituitary causes from ectopic ACTH production
Bricaire test is the best screening test for Cushing syndrome
Pituitary MRI should be recommended when ACTH independent Cushing syndrome is present
High ACTH levels usually suggest an ACTH secreting tumor

questions.note: FALSE: Cushing's disease = PITUITARY adenoma; Liddle 2×2 (low dose) confirms hypercortisolism, it is the HIGH dose (2×8) that separates pituitary from ectopic; pituitary MRI is for ACTH-DEPENDENT Cushing. The Bricaire test (1-mg overnight DST) IS a best screening test; high ACTH suggests an ACTH-secreting tumour.

questions.q: Treatment of Addison disease:

o.t: Consists of gluco- and mineralocorticoid therapy
Dietary sodium restriction is necessary because of the glucocorticoid therapy
Daily doses of hydrocortisone should be increased in periods of major stress
Treatment can be interrupted if high blood pressure occurs

questions.note: Addison: lifelong gluco- + mineralocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone), increased doses during stress; normal salt; never interrupt (reduce fludrocortisone if hypertension).

questions.q: Indications for testing for Conn's disease are:

o.t: Patients with high blood pressure that is not controlled with conventional therapy
High blood pressure that develops before the age of 40

questions.note: Screen for primary aldosteronism: resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced HYPOkalaemia, adrenal incidentaloma, hypertension < 40 y, sleep apnoea, family history of early stroke/PA.

questions.q: The classic physical finding in Addison's disease is:
questions.note: Hyperpigmentation (skin creases, scars, gums, nipples) is the classic physical finding of Addison's disease (ACTH/MSH excess).

questions.q: Acute adrenal crisis is characterized by:

o.t: Can be found in infants with congenital adrenal hypoplasia
In adults, it can be caused by unilateral adrenal hemorrhage
It is characterized by hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia
Treatment consists of IV glucose and saline solutions, as well as hydrocortisone IV
It can lead to hypotension and shock

questions.note: Adrenal crisis: in neonates (CAH, adrenal hypoplasia), bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen), stress in known Addison; hypotension/shock, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, HYPERkalaemia → IV hydrocortisone 100 mg + saline/glucose.

questions.q: The first choice treatment for Cushing's disease in a 49-year old male patient with a pituitary adenoma is:
questions.note: ACTH-dependent Cushing with pituitary microadenoma (Cushing's disease): transsphenoidal adenomectomy is first choice; pasireotide, ketoconazole/metyrapone, radiotherapy or bilateral adrenalectomy are second line.

questions.q: What diagnosis reveals the following hormonal changes: slightly increased ACTH, normal basal cortisol (8 o'clock), high nocturnal cortisol, cortisol after Liddle 2×8 decreased by more than 50% compared to basal cortisol at 8 o'clock?
questions.note: ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism suppressing by > 50 % on high-dose dexamethasone = Cushing's disease.

questions.q: The following disorders can evolve with hypertension (high BP):
questions.note: Endocrine hypertension: acromegaly, Cushing, Conn (primary aldosteronism), pheochromocytoma, primary hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism (systolic). Addison causes HYPOtension.

questions.q: nmol/L (N = 136–145 nmol/L), basal cortisol = 210 nmol/L and 60 min after Synacthen 250 microgram given IV = 330 nmol/L.

o.t: The most likely diagnosis is primary adrenocortical insufficiency
The most likely diagnosis is secondary adrenocortical insufficiency; however, the administration of hydrocortisone is not indicated because of heart failure
Additional useful investigation is determination of ACTH
Additional useful investigations are TSH + FT4

questions.note: Basal cortisol 210 nmol/L with peak 330 nmol/L (< 500) after Synacthen = adrenal insufficiency; ACTH determination distinguishes primary vs secondary, and TSH/FT4 look for associated thyroid (or pituitary) deficits. (Hydrocortisone is needed – its absence is not justified by heart failure; IV only in crisis.)

questions.q: Primary hyperaldosteronism:

o.t: Is characterized by hypo K⁺ and increased plasma renin activity
Clinically presents with asthenia, fatigability, muscle weakness, moderate/severe arterial hypertension
In cases of adrenal hyperplasia spironolactone is not indicated
The dosage of renin and aldosterone should always be performed within minutes of the transfer from ortostatism to clinostatism
In Conn's adenoma, the prognosis after surgery is excellent (healing)

questions.note: Primary aldosteronism: hypertension, hypokalaemia (muscle weakness, fatigue, polyuria), SUPPRESSED renin; bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone/eplerenone; aldosterone-producing adenoma → adrenalectomy (excellent prognosis). Sampling: upright, morning, after 2 h of ambulation.

questions.q: Therapeutic options for a patient with ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome include:
questions.note: ACTH-independent (adrenal) Cushing: adrenalectomy; steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, mitotane for carcinoma). Pasireotide and cabergoline act on pituitary corticotrophs; radiotherapy is for pituitary disease.

questions.q: In the treatment of Cushing's disease, one can use:
questions.note: Cushing's disease medical therapy: steroidogenesis inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat), pituitary-directed pasireotide and cabergoline, glucocorticoid receptor blocker mifepristone.

questions.q: Addison's disease is characterized by:
questions.note: Addison: low cortisol with HIGH ACTH (and low aldosterone, high renin).

questions.q: The following investigations are useful for diagnosis and evaluation of Cushing's syndrome:

o.t: Longer low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (2 mg/day for 48 h)

questions.note: Cushing work-up: screening by 1-mg overnight DST (Bricaire), 24-h urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol; confirmation by low-dose DST 2 mg/day × 2 days (Liddle 2×2); ACTH (dependent vs independent); high-dose DST (Liddle 2×8) for pituitary vs ectopic. The Synacthen test explores INSUFFICIENCY.

questions.q: Acute adrenal crisis is characterized by:
questions.note: Adrenal crisis: low cortisol, hyponatraemia, HYPERkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension.

questions.q: Features suggestive for Cushing syndrome are:
questions.note: Cushing: weight gain (central), depression/psychosis, acne, menstrual disturbances, hirsutism, hypertension, OSTEOPOROSIS (not osteomalacia).

questions.q: Primary hyperaldosteronism screening should be performed in the following cases:

o.t: Hypertension not controlled on 3 or more conventional antihypertensive medication
Hypertension developed before the age of 40

questions.note: Screen for primary aldosteronism: hypertension with spontaneous/diuretic hypokalaemia, resistant hypertension (≥ 3 drugs), onset < 40 y, ADRENAL (not pituitary) incidentaloma, sleep apnoea.

questions.q: The best screening test to diagnose Cushing syndrome is:
questions.note: The 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (Bricaire/Nugent) – with 24-h urinary free cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol – is a first-line screening test. Metyrapone and Synacthen tests explore adrenal reserve.

questions.q: Give the diagnosis for this profile: altered general condition, hypertension, hirsutism, severe hypokalaemia, LOW ACTH, normal 8 a.m. cortisol, high midnight cortisol, plasma cortisol after 8 mg dexamethasone decreased by LESS than 50 % of the 8 a.m. basal cortisol.
questions.note: ACTH-INDEPENDENT (low ACTH) hypercortisolism that does not suppress, with rapid deterioration, androgen excess (hirsutism) and mineralocorticoid effects (severe hypokalaemia, hypertension) = adrenocortical carcinoma (mixed secretion). Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous cortisol. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Primary hyperaldosteronism:

o.t: Is characterised by hypokalaemia and increased plasma renin activity
Clinically presents with asthenia, fatigability, muscle weakness, moderate–severe hypertension
In adrenal hyperplasia, spironolactone is indicated
Renin and aldosterone should always be measured a few minutes after moving from standing to lying
In Conn's adenoma, the prognosis after surgery is excellent

questions.note: Primary aldosteronism: hypertension, hypokalaemia (weakness, cramps, polyuria), SUPPRESSED renin (high aldosterone/renin ratio, measured in the morning after ≥ 2 h upright). Bilateral hyperplasia → mineralocorticoid antagonists; adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy (cure of hypokalaemia, BP improved). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 34-year-old patient gained 15 kg in a year, with raised BP and lumbar back pain. Exam: axillary acanthosis nigricans, central obesity, red striae on the lower abdomen. Raised 24-h urinary free cortisol, basal cortisol 26 µg/dL, ACTH at the upper limit of normal. After 1 mg dexamethasone cortisol is 4 µg/dL, after 8 mg dexamethasone cortisol is 3 µg/dL. True statements:

o.t: The most likely diagnosis is a paraneoplastic syndrome (bronchial carcinoid)
The most likely diagnosis is Cushing's disease
The most likely diagnosis is ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome
Further investigation with a thoraco-abdominal CT is appropriate
Further investigation with a pituitary MRI is appropriate

questions.note: Hypercortisolism (high UFC, no suppression with 1 mg) that is ACTH-dependent (normal-high ACTH) and suppresses by > 50 % with 8 mg dexamethasone (26 → 3) = Cushing's disease → pituitary MRI (± inferior petrosal sinus sampling). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The following signs suggest Cushing's syndrome:
questions.note: Cushing: central (facio-truncal) obesity, thin skin with purple striae and bruising, proximal muscle ATROPHY/weakness, hirsutism, HYPERtension. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Biological signs of Cushing's disease are:

o.t: Loss of the circadian cortisol rhythm
No response to the low-dose dexamethasone test
No response to the high-dose dexamethasone test

questions.note: Cushing's disease: high urinary free cortisol, lost nycthemeral rhythm (high midnight cortisol), no suppression on low-dose DST, normal-to-high ACTH, but SUPPRESSION (> 50 %) on high-dose DST. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of Cushing's disease:

o.t: Removal of the adenoma by the transsphenoidal route
Removal of the adenoma by laparoscopy
Bilateral adrenalectomy in case of failure or recurrence after adenomectomy

questions.note: Cushing's disease: transsphenoidal adenomectomy first; if it fails: repeat surgery, pituitary radiotherapy, medical therapy (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, pasireotide) or bilateral adrenalectomy (risk of Nelson syndrome). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Adrenal insufficiencies:

o.t: Are primary from destruction of both adrenals (Addison's disease) or secondary to hypothalamic-pituitary ACTH deficiency
In secondary forms there is skin hyperpigmentation
Untreated evolution is more severe in Addison's disease than in hypopituitarism
Untreated or unrecognised, hypocorticism is fatal through adrenal crisis

questions.note: Adrenal insufficiency: chronic or acute; primary (Addison) or secondary (ACTH deficiency). Secondary forms have PALLOR (no ACTH excess) and keep aldosterone, so they are less severe. Untreated, adrenal crisis is fatal. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical signs suggestive of Addison's disease are:
questions.note: Addison: fatigue (worse in the evening), weight loss, anorexia, nausea, HYPOtension (orthostatic), hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hypoglycaemia. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Hormonal tests in Addison's disease show:

o.t: Low or very low basal cortisol
No or weak response to stimulation (Synacthen)

questions.note: Addison: low cortisol, absent rise after Synacthen (ACTH stimulation – the original item wrongly says "dexamethasone"), low aldosterone with high renin, very high ACTH, HYPOglycaemia. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of Addison's disease:

o.t: Must be continued for life and never stopped
The dose must be doubled or tripled in infection, trauma, labour and delivery
Monitoring relies on clinical status, blood pressure, weight and serum electrolytes

questions.note: Addison: lifelong hydrocortisone (≈ 15–25 mg/day today; 20–40 mg/day in older texts) + fludrocortisone, increased in stress, NORMAL salt; monitoring is clinical + BP, weight, electrolytes (renin). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical picture of hypercortisolism:
questions.note: Cushing's syndrome: moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, striae, bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Medical treatment of hypercortisolism:
questions.note: Steroidogenesis inhibitors: ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, mitotane (o,p'-DDD – adrenolytic, adrenocortical carcinoma), etomidate IV. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Virilisation syndrome:

o.t: In girls results in clitoral hypertrophy
Short final stature with early growth-plate fusion

questions.note: Androgen excess (CAH, tumours): clitoromegaly, hirsutism, deep voice, muscle; in boys: isosexual precocious pseudopuberty (macrogenitosomia); advanced bone age with short final height. Salt LOSS in classic 21-OH deficiency (retention in 11β-OH deficiency). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathies (APS):

o.t: The main forms are APS 2 and APS 4
Hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency are found in the frequent form
Thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes are found in the rare form

questions.note: APS1 (APECED, AIRE gene, rare): candidiasis + hypoparathyroidism + Addison. APS2 (Schmidt, the frequent form): Addison + autoimmune thyroid disease ± type 1 diabetes. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In untreated permanent hypertension, all the following may exist in primary aldosteronism (Conn adenoma) EXCEPT one:

o.t: Usually good tolerance of the hypertension

questions.note: Conn: hypertension, hypokalaemia → muscle weakness/paralysis, polyuria (nephrogenic), metabolic alkalosis → tetany/paraesthesias; NO oedema (aldosterone escape). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: All the following belong to acute primary adrenal insufficiency EXCEPT one:
questions.note: Adrenal insufficiency: asthenia, hypotension, weight loss, depression/apathy, GI symptoms, salt craving; polydipsia is not a feature (it suggests DI, diabetes, hypercalcaemia). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Klinefelter Syndrome:

o.t: The testes are constantly present in the scrotum
Seminiferous tubules are affected by a sclerohyalinosis process
PRL is always elevated and explains gynecomastia
The testes are reduced to two fibrous bands

questions.note: Klinefelter (47,XXY): small firm testes (in the scrotum) with sclero-hyalinosis of the seminiferous tubules → azoospermia; high FSH/LH, low testosterone; gynaecomastia from the high oestradiol/testosterone ratio. Fibrous streaks = Turner.

questions.q: Turner Syndrome is characterized by:

o.t: Possible cardiac, vascular, and renal malformations

questions.note: Turner (45,X0): short stature (SHOX haplo-insufficiency, not GH deficiency), gonadal dysgenesis with PRIMARY amenorrhoea, coarctation/bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney. No virilisation, normal intelligence usually.

questions.q: Kallmann Syndrome:

o.t: Is a form of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
Is caused by a hypothalamic GnRH deficiency
Is caused by a deficiency in testosterone secretion at the testicular level
The diagnosis is confirmed by identifying the genetic mutation

questions.note: Kallmann syndrome = congenital isolated GnRH deficiency (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) with anosmia/hyposmia (olfactory bulb agenesis). Diagnosis is clinical-hormonal (low LH/FSH, low sex steroids, MRI); a mutation is found only in a minority (KAL1/ANOS1, FGFR1…).

questions.q: The hormonal profile of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is represented by:
questions.note: Hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism: gonad failure → low oestradiol/testosterone, HIGH FSH and LH (loss of negative feedback).

questions.q: A 31-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea. The first-line tests are:
questions.note: Secondary amenorrhoea: first exclude pregnancy (β-hCG), then prolactin (and TSH), followed by FSH/LH/oestradiol and the progesterone test.

questions.q: A 23-year-old man presents with tall stature, gynecomastia, decreased libido, and low testosterone levels.

o.t: FSH, LH, and karyotype are useful tests for the final and differential diagnosis
Prolactin dosage is a useful test for the final and differential diagnosis
If Klinefelter syndrome is confirmed, infertility is the rule
If Klinefelter syndrome is confirmed, stimulation by injections of gonadotropins (FSH and hCG) can be used for spermatogenesis induction
Treatment is represented by androgen substitution

questions.note: Tall man + gynaecomastia + low testosterone = suspect Klinefelter: FSH/LH (high) and karyotype (47,XXY) confirm; infertility (azoospermia) is the rule – gonadotropins are useless (primary testicular failure), testicular sperm extraction for IVF is possible; testosterone replacement.

questions.q: Which of the following are characteristic to ovarian failure with prepubertal onset?
questions.note: Ovarian failure before puberty: sexual infantilism – primary amenorrhoea, absent thelarche, infantile uterus, eunuchoid proportions (tall, long limbs) because of delayed epiphyseal closure. Short stature only in Turner.

questions.q: Which of the following are characteristic for Turner's syndrome?

o.t: It is a syndrome of gonadal dysgenesis
It should be used in the therapy plan

questions.note: Turner: gonadal dysgenesis (streak gonads), short stature – GH IS used in therapy to improve final height (although GH/IGF-1 are normal); no exophthalmos.

questions.q: The Wolffian ducts differentiate into:

o.t: The upper third of the vagina

questions.note: Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts, under testosterone → epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts. Müllerian ducts → tubes, uterus, upper vagina; testes come from the gonadal ridge.

questions.q: What does Luteinizing Hormone do in men and women?

o.t: Men – supports sperm production and women – promotes egg development
Men – promotes lutein production and women – promotes lutein production
Men – stimulates Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone and women – induces ovulation and promotes the activity of the corpus luteum
Men – promotes melanin production and women – promotes melanin production
Men – supports sperm production and women – promotes follicle growth

questions.note: LH: in men stimulates Leydig cells → testosterone; in women triggers ovulation (LH surge) and maintains the corpus luteum (progesterone). FSH → spermatogenesis (Sertoli) / follicle growth.

questions.q: Primary ovary insufficiency with pre- pubertal onset is characterized by:
questions.note: Prepubertal primary ovarian failure: sexual infantilism, PRIMARY amenorrhoea, eunuchoid habitus, HIGH gonadotropins.

questions.q: From the characteristics below, circle ONLY the ones which are specific for primary male hypogonadism with pre-pubertal onset:

o.t: Delicate facial skin, fine with wrinkles in the corners of the mouth and eyes

questions.note: Prepubertal primary male hypogonadism (eunuchoidism): poor muscles, gynoid (female) fat distribution, fine skin with perioral/periorbital wrinkles, sparse facial hair, high-pitched voice, eunuchoid proportions (arm span > height, lower segment > upper).

questions.q: The first test for investigating secondary amenorrhea is:
questions.note: The first test in any secondary amenorrhoea is the pregnancy test (β-hCG).

questions.q: The Turner syndrome is characterized by:

o.t: Short neck with low hair insertion on the back head

questions.note: Turner: short stature, webbed/short neck with low posterior hairline, shield chest, cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpal, sexual infantilism (no puberty), usually normal intelligence.

questions.q: A 31-year-old man is presenting with a revealing 10×10⁶ sperm/ml with 42% of them exhibiting progressive motility and 30% normal morphology. Which are the next steps?

o.t: Reassure the patient – his semen analysis is just decreased sperm motility
Repeat semen analysis to confirm oligospermia
Refer him for testicular biopsy and scrotal US

questions.note: 10 million/mL = oligozoospermia (< 15 million): repeat the semen analysis (≥ 2 samples 2–3 months apart) and measure FSH, LH, testosterone; prolactin if low testosterone/libido; biopsy is not first line.

questions.q: Kallmann syndrome:

o.t: Is a form of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
Is caused by hypothalamic GnRH deficiency
Is caused by a deficiency of testicular testosterone secretion
The diagnosis is certified by highlighting the genetic mutation

questions.note: Kallmann = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from GnRH deficiency + anosmia; genetic confirmation in only a minority.

questions.q: The hormonal profile of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is represented by:

o.t: High levels of LH, low levels of LH

questions.note: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: low oestradiol, HIGH FSH and LH.

questions.q: In Klinefelter's Syndrome:

o.t: The testes are constantly present in the scrotum
Seminiferous tubules are affected by sclerosis and hyalinosis process
Prolactin is always elevated, explaining gynecomastia
Testes are reduced to two fibrous bands
Testes have a normal volume and consistency

questions.note: Klinefelter: small firm testes in the scrotum with tubular sclero-hyalinosis; gynaecomastia from high oestradiol (prolactin is normal); fibrous streaks = Turner.

questions.q: Treatment in primary ovarian insufficiency with onset before puberty is:
questions.note: Prepubertal ovarian failure: progressive oestrogen (then oestro-progestative) replacement to induce puberty; GH if Turner; ovulation induction is impossible (no follicles).

questions.q: The LH is responsible for:

o.t: In men – stimulates spermatogenesis; in women – promotes follicular maturation
Stimulation of lutein synthesis in both sexes
In men – stimulation of testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells; in women – triggers ovulation, stimulates progesterone synthesis, prepares uterine endometrium for possible pregnancy
Control of anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) biosynthesis in both sexes

questions.note: LH: Leydig cell testosterone in men; ovulation, corpus luteum progesterone in women.

questions.q: Useful tests to investigate secondary amenorrhea are:
questions.note: Secondary amenorrhoea work-up: pregnancy test, prolactin, TSH, FSH/LH (+ oestradiol), progesterone challenge, pelvic ultrasound; scintigraphy has no role.

questions.q: Causes of primary male hypogonadism include:
questions.note: Primary (testicular) hypogonadism: Klinefelter, anorchia/cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemotherapy/radiation, trauma. Hyperprolactinaemia, head trauma and pituitary adenoma cause SECONDARY (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism.

questions.q: Turner syndrome is characterized by:

o.t: Amenorrhea with absence of uterus and ovaries

questions.note: Turner: short stature, absent breast development (no puberty), primary amenorrhoea with streak gonads; the uterus is present (small, infantile). Anosmia = Kallmann.

questions.q: Androgen deficiency is manifested by:

o.t: Absent or very sparse axillary and pubic hair

questions.note: Prepubertal androgen deficiency: delayed bone age, tall eunuchoid stature (delayed epiphyseal closure), small testes, sparse body hair, poor muscle mass.

questions.q: Turner syndrome is characterized by:
questions.note: Turner: ptosis, epicanthus, micrognathia (not prognathism), high-arched palate, cubitus valgus, webbed neck, short stature.

questions.q: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by:
questions.note: Klinefelter: tall stature with eunuchoid proportions, small firm testes, infertility (azoospermia), gynaecomastia, osteoporosis (androgen deficiency).

questions.q: Clinical and hormonal signs in PCOS:
questions.note: PCOS: oligo/anovulation (infertility), hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne; raised total/free testosterone, ± DHEA-S), LOW SHBG (insulin resistance), raised LH/FSH ratio, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Thyroid function is normal. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: LH is responsible for:

o.t: In men stimulating spermatogenesis; in women promoting follicular maturation
Stimulation of lutein synthesis in both sexes
In men stimulating testosterone synthesis in the Leydig cells
In women triggering ovulation and stimulating progesterone synthesis
Preparing the uterine endometrium for a possible pregnancy

questions.note: LH: Leydig cells → testosterone; in women: LH surge → ovulation, corpus luteum → progesterone. FSH drives spermatogenesis/follicle growth; the endometrium is prepared by oestradiol and progesterone, not directly by LH. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The hormonal profile of HYPOgonadotropic hypogonadism is:

o.t: Low oestradiol in women and low testosterone in men

questions.note: Hypogonadotropic (central/secondary) hypogonadism: low (or inappropriately normal) LH and FSH with low sex steroids – hypothalamic (Kallmann, functional amenorrhoea) or pituitary (tumour, hyperprolactinaemia) cause. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Treatment of primary ovarian insufficiency with POST-pubertal onset is:
questions.note: Premature ovarian insufficiency: hormone replacement with oestrogen + progestin (cyclic) until the age of natural menopause – protects bone and cardiovascular system and treats symptoms; fertility via egg donation. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Primary ovarian insufficiency:

o.t: Is characterised biologically by raised FSH and LH
Oestradiol is low or very low
Before puberty it presents as primary amenorrhoea with absent puberty
After puberty it presents as secondary amenorrhoea with hot flushes

questions.note: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: high FSH/LH, low oestradiol; physiological model = menopause; prepubertal onset → primary amenorrhoea + sexual infantilism; postpubertal → secondary amenorrhoea, hot flushes (POI < 40 y). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Turner syndrome is characterised by:

o.t: Absence of the Y chromosome in all cells

questions.note: Turner: 45,X (or mosaic/structural X anomalies) – short stature, dysmorphism, gonadal dysgenesis with primary amenorrhoea and sexual infantilism. Y material may be present in some mosaics (gonadoblastoma risk → gonadectomy). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical signs of polycystic ovary syndrome:

o.t: Hirsutism starting at puberty and progressing

questions.note: PCOS: oligo/amenorrhoea, anovulatory infertility, hirsutism/acne from puberty, android obesity, insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical signs of male hypogonadism:

o.t: Tall stature with long limbs (macroskelia) if onset is before puberty
Growth delay may be seen in hypothalamic-pituitary (central) forms
In adulthood secondary sexual characteristics regress
Libido and erectile function are normal

questions.note: Male hypogonadism: small testes, decreased libido and erectile dysfunction, loss of body hair and muscle, osteoporosis; prepubertal onset → eunuchoid tall stature (delayed epiphyseal closure); central forms with GH deficit may have short stature. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The second part of the luteal phase is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT one:

o.t: Decreased GnRH pulse frequency leading to lower FSH
Increased GnRH pulse frequency leading to FSH production

questions.note: Late luteal phase: luteolysis → oestradiol and progesterone fall, which releases GnRH pulse frequency → FSH rises to recruit the next cohort (luteal-follicular transition). Decreasing GnRH frequency with falling FSH is NOT a feature. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In postmenopausal women we find:
questions.note: Oestrogen loss after menopause raises total and LDL cholesterol (and triglyceride-rich VLDL), lowers HDL → increased cardiovascular risk. (Translated from the French section.)

cards.q: Primary vs secondary disease – how do the hormones move?
cards.a: Primary (gland): end hormone and trophic hormone move in OPPOSITE directions. Secondary/tertiary: both move in the SAME direction.

cards.q: Which pituitary hormone is under tonic inhibition?
cards.a: Prolactin (dopamine). Stalk section → PRL ↑, all others ↓.

cards.q: Suspected deficiency vs excess – which dynamic test?
cards.a: Deficiency → stimulation test; excess → suppression test.

cards.q: Most common pituitary adenoma and its first-line treatment?
cards.a: Prolactinoma → cabergoline (even macroadenoma with chiasm compression).
IGF-1 ↑ + OGTT: GH not suppressed below 1 ng/mL; then pituitary MRI.

cards.q: Order of hormone loss in hypopituitarism?
Which deficiency to replace first in panhypopituitarism?

cards.a: Primary polydipsia concentrates; central DI concentrates only after desmopressin; nephrogenic DI never.
Agalactia (failure of lactation) + no resumption of menses after postpartum haemorrhage.

cards.q: Best single screening test of thyroid function?
Thyroid nodule with LOW TSH – next test?
Suspicious ultrasound features of a nodule?
cards.a: Marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide, extrathyroidal extension.

cards.q: Thyroid cancer with calcitonin as marker?
Painful thyroid + fever + high ESR + low uptake?

cards.a: IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone, warming, ventilatory support.

cards.q: Most serious side effect of thionamides?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis – sore throat + fever → stop drug, CBC.
PTU/thiamazole first, iodine ≥ 1 h later, propranolol, hydrocortisone.
Pregnancy/breastfeeding; active moderate–severe orbitopathy without steroid cover.

cards.q: Most common cause of hypercalcaemia: outpatient vs hospital?
Hypocalcaemia with HIGH PTH and Albright osteodystrophy?

cards.a: MEN1: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas. MEN2A: medullary thyroid, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid.

cards.q: Hyperpigmentation – primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency?
Best screening tests for Cushing syndrome?
cards.a: 1-mg overnight DST (Bricaire), 24-h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol.
Cushing DISEASE (pituitary); ectopic ACTH does not suppress.
Congenital GnRH deficiency + anosmia → hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
45,X: short stature, streak gonads, primary amenorrhoea, coarctation, horseshoe kidney.
47,XXY: tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, azoospermia, high FSH/LH.
Pregnancy test (β-hCG), then prolactin and TSH.

cards.q: What does LH do in men and women?
cards.a: Men: Leydig testosterone. Women: ovulation + corpus luteum progesterone.
Epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts.
